docs.title: 3.1 Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA)
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook stores personally identifiable information — email address, full name, optional student number, degree and year of study — plus user-authored content (projects, entries, tags). Under POPIA we act as the responsible party for this data. That creates obligations including:

  • Purpose specification — data must be collected for a defined, lawful purpose. Ours is the operation of the logbook the user signed up for.
  • Minimality — only data necessary for the purpose. Every profile field is optional; an account is usable with just an email and password.
  • Security safeguards — "appropriate, reasonable technical and organisational measures" to prevent loss, damage or unauthorised access.
  • Data subject participation — users must be able to access and correct their data, and to have it deleted.
  • Breach notification — if a breach occurs, the Information Regulator and affected data subjects must be notified.
  • Cross-border transfer — data must not leave South Africa without an adequate level of protection.

Specific exposures in this project:

  • The database is hosted on Neon in the United States (us-east-2). This is a cross-border transfer of personal information. In a production deployment we would need to document the legal basis, or use a region within South Africa.
  • Emails are delivered through Resend, or Gmail's SMTP service when Resend is not configured. Recipient addresses and email contents traverse that provider's infrastructure.

docs.title: 3.2 Consumer Protection Act
docs.text: The right to cancel and the right to fair value, good quality and safety create a practical obligation: a user must be able to remove their data on request. Our account deletion flow (§4.6) satisfies this.

docs.title: 3.3 Electronic Communications and Transactions Act (ECTA)
docs.text: ECTA governs electronic signatures and records. Our session tokens are not signatures, but the acceptance of the user's password at account creation and every subsequent login constitutes an electronic transaction. We keep auditable records through Prisma's created_at and updated_at columns.

docs.title: 3.4 Common-law duty of care
docs.text: Independent of statute, a service that accepts and stores credentials owes its users a duty of reasonable care. Negligently weak password storage, absent encryption of 2FA secrets, or a hardcoded JWT secret would breach this duty and expose the project to a civil claim after a breach.

docs.title: 3.5 Academic-integrity exposure
docs.text: The brief requires "established libraries, not your own authentication system." A submission that either rolled its own cryptography or delegated everything to a provider would be non-compliant even if functionally correct. §5 addresses how this project sits within that boundary.

docs.title: 4. Precautions in the implementation
docs.text: Every precaution below refers to a specific line of code, not a general principle.

docs.title: 4.1 Password storage
docs.text:
From utils/auth.ts:

export async function hashPassword(password: string): Promise<string> {
  const salt = await bcrypt.genSalt(10);
  return bcrypt.hash(password, salt);
}

export async function comparePassword(password: string, hash: string): Promise<boolean> {
  return bcrypt.compare(password, hash);
}
  • bcryptjs with cost factor 10. The work factor is exponential: each increment doubles the time to test a guess. A cost of 10 takes approximately 100 ms per hash on current server hardware, which makes offline brute-force against the database expensive without noticeably slowing sign-in.
  • Per-password salt. bcrypt.genSalt produces a fresh random salt for every account. Two users with the same password produce different hashes, and precomputed rainbow tables do not apply.
  • The plain password is never stored. hashPassword is called inside /register and /reset-password; the return value is what reaches the database. Nothing else in the code path logs, serialises or transmits the raw password.
  • Constant-time comparison. bcrypt.compare reads the salt embedded in the stored hash, re-hashes the incoming password with it, and compares the two digests. It is the library's constant-time implementation, not a string comparison in our code.

docs.title: 4.2 Session tokens
docs.text:
From utils/auth.ts:

const configuredSecret = process.env.JWT_SECRET;

if (!configuredSecret && process.env.NODE_ENV === "production") {
  throw new Error("JWT_SECRET is not set. Refusing to start in production...");
}

const JWT_SECRET = configuredSecret ?? randomBytes(48).toString("hex");

export function generateToken(userId: string): string {
  return jwt.sign({ userId }, JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: "7d" });
}
  • Secret is environment-supplied. JWT_SECRET comes from the process environment, never from a value written into the repository. The pre-fix fallback "your-fallback-secret-key" was removed in the course of the project; the current code refuses to start in production without a secret.
  • Startup refusal. A misconfigured production deployment fails loudly on boot rather than silently signing sessions with a key the world can read.
  • Random fallback outside production. Development environments generate a fresh 48-byte secret at process start. Sessions do not survive a restart, but no predictable key is ever used.
  • Seven-day expiry. Every session token carries an exp claim. A stolen token has a bounded useful life.
  • Purpose-scoped claims. OAuth state tokens and 2FA-pending tokens are signed with the same key but carry a purpose claim, and verifyToken rejects any token whose purpose is not the default. An OAuth state token cannot be replayed as a session even though it validates cryptographically:
if (payload.purpose !== undefined || typeof payload.userId !== "string") return null;

docs.title: 4.3 Middleware boundary
docs.text:
From middleware/auth.middleware.ts:

export function requireAuth(req, res, next) {
  const authHeader = req.headers.authorization;
  if (!authHeader || !authHeader.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "Unauthorized access: Token missing" });
  }
  const token = authHeader.split(" ")[1];
  const decoded = verifyToken(token);
  if (!decoded) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: "Unauthorized access: Invalid or expired token" });
  }
  req.userId = decoded.userId;
  next();
}
  • Single point of enforcement. Every protected route passes through this middleware. There is one implementation of "is this session valid," not one per route.
  • req.userId is derived from the verified token, never from the request body or query. A caller cannot claim to be another user.
  • No session table. JWTs are stateless. This is fast, but means individual token revocation is not possible before expiry. §5.2 discusses the trade-off.

docs.title: 4.4 Two-factor authentication
docs.text:
Two-factor authentication is opt-in and TOTP-based, compatible with Google Authenticator, Authy and any RFC 6238 client.

Secret encryption. The TOTP secret is encrypted before storage (see utils/twoFactorSecret.ts, invoked from auth.routes.ts). A database reader who finds the column cannot derive valid TOTP codes. The /2fa/setup endpoint refuses to proceed if the encryption key is not present:

if (!hasEncryptionKey()) {
  return res.status(503).json({
    error: "Two-factor authentication is unavailable: the server is missing its encryption key...",
  });
}

This is a deliberate design decision: failing closed rather than storing an unprotected secret.

Second-step binding (BUG-006). /login does not issue a session when 2FA is enabled. It issues a short-lived token whose purpose is 2fa-pending:

return res.json({
  requiresTwoFactor: true,
  email: user.email,
  twoFactorToken: generateTwoFactorPendingToken(user.id),
});

/login/2fa accepts only that token as proof the password step happened:

const userId = verifyTwoFactorPendingToken(twoFactorToken);
if (!userId) {
  return res.status(401).json({ error: "Your sign-in session has expired..." });
}

The pending token expires in five minutes — long enough to read a code off a phone, short enough to be useless if intercepted and held.

Recovery codes (BUG-005). When 2FA is enabled the user receives ten single-use recovery codes. Only SHA-256 digests are stored; the raw codes exist only in the enable response and cannot be retrieved later. Codes are consumed through an atomic update:

const { count } = await prisma.twoFactorRecoveryCode.updateMany({
  where: { userId, codeHash: hashRecoveryCode(code), usedAt: null },
  data: { usedAt: new Date() },
});
return count === 1;

The usedAt: null guard lives inside the UPDATE. Two concurrent requests with the same code cannot both succeed: the database applies the predicate atomically and only one caller sees a row count of 1.

docs.title: 4.5 Email token handling
docs.text:
From auth.routes.ts:

const verificationToken = generateRawToken();
const verificationExpiry = new Date(Date.now() + 3600000);

const user = await prisma.user.create({
  data: {
    ...
    emailVerificationToken: hashToken(verificationToken),
    emailVerificationExpiry: verificationExpiry,
  },
});
  • The stored value is a digest, not the raw token. A database read cannot be turned into a verification of the attacker's own email.
  • One-hour expiry. Both the verification token and the reset token are valid for one hour.
  • Single use. Both are nulled or deleted upon consumption. The reset flow also deletes every other reset row for that user in a single transaction, so a leaked token from an earlier request cannot be used after a later reset has completed.

Reset tokens are deleted transactionally:

await prisma.$transaction([
  prisma.user.update({ where: { id: resetRecord.userId }, data: { passwordHash: newPasswordHash } }),
  prisma.passwordReset.deleteMany({ where: { userId: resetRecord.userId } }),
]);

Either both operations commit or neither does. A half-completed reset cannot leave a consumed token behind.

docs.title: 4.6 Account deletion (30-day grace period)
docs.text:
The DELETE /account handler does not remove the user immediately. It sets scheduled_deletion_at to midnight thirty days out:

const scheduledDeletionAt = user.scheduledDeletionAt ?? (() => {
  const d = new Date();
  d.setDate(d.getDate() + 30);
  d.setHours(0, 0, 0, 0);
  return d;
})();
  • Re-confirmed with the password. Holding a valid session is not sufficient to start a deletion. A stolen token cannot trigger it.
  • Email notice. sendDeletionScheduledEmail informs the user with the exact date so the decision is visible and reversible.
  • Cancel endpoint. POST /account/cancel-deletion clears the timestamp. A user who changes their mind signs back in and the deletion is cancelled by a distinct, explicit action.
  • Cascade. The User model carries onDelete: Cascade on its relations, so when the purge runs, projects, entries, tags and 2FA codes are removed together.
  • Purge job. A scheduled task sweeps expired deletions hourly and on startup. Login also checks the timestamp, so a user whose grace period has already expired cannot sign in while the sweep is pending.

docs.title: 4.7 Rate limiting
docs.text:
From rateLimit.middleware.ts:

Limiter Window Limit Applies to loginLimiter 15 min 20 /login twoFactorLimiter 15 min 10 /login/2fa registerLimiter 60 min 5 /register authLimiter 15 min 100 All auth routes (headers) assistantLimiter 10 min 30 Help assistant
  • Password guessing is bounded. Twenty attempts per IP per 15 minutes means a brute force attack against an 8-character password is infeasible.
  • TOTP brute force is bounded more tightly. A six-digit code is one million possibilities; ten attempts per 15 minutes means an attacker exhausts less than 0.001% of the space per day.
  • Registration spam is bounded. Five accounts per IP per hour.

Rate limiting can be disabled in tests through RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED, and by default is off under NODE_ENV=test. This keeps the auth suite fast without weakening production.

docs.title: 4.8 Email enumeration resistance
docs.text:
The /forgot-password handler responds identically whether or not the email exists:

if (!user) {
  return res.json({ message: "If account exists, a password reset email has been sent." });
}

/login returns "Invalid email or password" for both a missing account and a wrong password. An attacker cannot distinguish the two cases through the API and use that distinction to enumerate valid accounts.

docs.title: 4.9 HTTPS and transport
docs.text: In production, the frontend is served over HTTPS by Cloudflare Pages and the API by Render's TLS-terminating proxy. Passwords, tokens and email links traverse the network encrypted. Local development runs over plain HTTP on localhost, which is acceptable because the loopback interface is not reachable by other hosts.

docs.title: 4.10 Secret management
docs.text:
Every secret lives in an environment variable that is never committed:

Variable Purpose JWT_SECRET Signs session tokens TWO_FACTOR_ENCRYPTION_KEY Encrypts TOTP secrets at rest RESEND_API_KEY, RESEND_FROM Sends verification, reset and deletion emails through Resend GMAIL_USER, GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD The Gmail SMTP fallback when Resend is not set DATABASE_URL Prisma connection string APP_URL Base URL for links in emails

.env is listed in .gitignore. In production the same variables are set in the Render dashboard.

docs.title: 5. Pros and cons of the self-hosted approach
5.1 Advantages
docs.text:
• Full control of data. Email addresses, hashes and TOTP secrets stay in our PostgreSQL instance. We decide retention, region and deletion timing. A provider would store equivalent data on our behalf and under their terms.
  • Full control of flow. Account deletion with a 30-day grace period is uncommon; most providers offer "delete now." Our design gives users a reversible window and sends an email at the moment of scheduling. That is a product decision we would not have been able to make with Auth0.
  • No vendor lock-in. If Neon, Render or Cloudflare went offline tomorrow, the code would run anywhere Node and PostgreSQL run. A JWT session issued on one deployment is valid on another, provided the secret matches.
  • Cost. bcryptjs, jsonwebtoken, otplib and nodemailer are free. At scale they would still be free; per-user pricing does not apply.
  • Alignment with the brief. The brief says "You must design and implement your API" and "you may not write your own authentication system." Our implementation does the first and demonstrably avoids the second by using libraries for every primitive.
  • Direct experience. Every trade-off in this document reflects a decision the team made and can defend. A provider solution would have hidden the same decisions behind a UI.

docs.title: 5.2 Disadvantages
docs.text:
• We own the failures. The audit trail of this project includes several bug reports whose fixes appear in this document — BUG-002 (hardcoded JWT secret), BUG-004 (unencrypted TOTP secrets), BUG-005 (no recovery codes), BUG-006 (2FA step not bound to the password step). Each was a real weakness until it was closed. A provider would have prevented those specific bugs at the cost of removing our ability to fix others.
  • No session revocation list. JWTs are valid until they expire. If a user reports a stolen laptop, we cannot revoke a specific token — the attacker keeps access for up to seven days. A session table would allow per-device logout, at the cost of a database lookup on every request. Auth0 provides this as a feature.
  • No device management. Users cannot see "you are signed in on 4 devices" and remove one. That is out of scope for this project.
  • No WebAuthn or SSO. Users cannot sign in with Google, GitHub or a hardware key. Adding Google OAuth would reduce password reliance, but it would also mean Google becomes an identity provider for our accounts, blurring the boundary the brief draws.
  • No breach-list check. We do not consult Have I Been Pwned or an equivalent to reject known-compromised passwords at signup. A library like zxcvbn or a HIBP API call would close this gap.
  • No password rotation or expiry. Users can keep the same password indefinitely. NIST guidance currently discourages forced rotation, so this is not considered a weakness, but it is a departure from what some auditors expect.
  • Limited audit trail. We do not log successful logins, failed logins, 2FA challenges or password resets in a way that would answer "was this account accessed on 3 October?" That would be a large addition and out of scope.
  • Operational fragility. Every deployment must set six environment variables correctly. A missing JWT_SECRET in production means no one can sign in. A missing email provider key (RESEND_API_KEY, or the Gmail pair) means no one receives verification emails. A provider would handle these centrally.

docs.title: 5.3 Comparison table
docs.text: Concern Digital Logbook (self-hosted) Auth0 / Google Sign-In Password hashing bcryptjs, our DB Vendor's Session tokens JWT, our keys Vendor's 2FA otplib, our secrets Vendor's Recovery codes Our implementation Vendor's Account recovery Email link we send Vendor sends Session revocation Not possible Supported Breach-list check Not implemented Often provided WebAuthn Not implemented Supported Audit logs Not implemented Provided SSO convenience None One-click Data controller for POPIA Us Joint with vendor Cross-border transfer Neon us-east-2 Vendor's regions Vendor lock-in None Significant Cost at scale Free Per-user Brief compliance Full Ambiguous — vendor owns auth

docs.title: 6. Residual risk and future work
docs.text:
Even after every precaution in §4, the following residual risks remain:

  • Region. Neon is hosted in the United States. For POPIA compliance in a real deployment we would either move to a South African region or document the legal basis for the transfer.
  • No compromise detection. We do not alert on failed login spikes or password reset bursts.
  • No account lockout. Repeated failed logins are rate-limited but the account itself is never locked. This is deliberate — lockout is a denial-of-service vector — but it is a design choice.
  • Secret rotation. JWT_SECRET can be rotated, but doing so invalidates every active session. There is no rolling rotation scheme.
  • TOTP window. otplib's default acceptance window of one step means a code is valid for approximately 90 seconds. A stricter window would reduce the interceptability but increase failed attempts.

Future work in a production system would address each of these; none is required by the project brief.

docs.title: 7. Conclusion
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook implements authentication using established libraries called from endpoints the team wrote. No cryptographic primitive is implemented by us: bcryptjs does password hashing, jsonwebtoken does session tokens, otplib does TOTP, and resend (or nodemailer over Gmail SMTP) delivers email. The current implementation reflects a running list of bug fixes that closed specific weaknesses — a hardcoded JWT secret, unencrypted TOTP secrets, unbound 2FA steps, and absent recovery codes — each of which is documented in the project's issue tracker.

The legal liabilities are those of any service that stores credentials and PII: POPIA obligations, a duty of reasonable care, and the practical requirement that users can delete their accounts. The precautions in §4 address each of these with a specific, code-level mitigation. The remaining disadvantages — no session revocation, no SSO, no audit log — are the price of running the system ourselves, and each has a well-understood fix that a production deployment would apply.

The brief's requirement that we use libraries rather than build our own authentication is satisfied. The brief's requirement that we design and implement our own API is satisfied. This document records both.

docs.text: This document tracks requirements, Q&A, and decisions made in consultation with the client (lecturers/TAs). It serves as project methodology evidence and records how client feedback influenced the development of the Digital Logbook.

docs.title: [Date: 2026-08-17] — Requirements Clarification Meeting
docs.text:
• Channel: Requirements Review Meeting.

  • Attendees: Client / Lecturer, Development Team (all members).

docs.title: 1. Project Ownership & Naming
docs.text:
• Client Decision: A project is strictly owned by a single student. Project names must be unique for each student (e.g., a student cannot have two projects named "CS Lab 1").

  • Impact:

  • projects table uses user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE.

  • Unique constraint: UNIQUE(user_id, name).

docs.title: 2. Project Archiving Behavior (US05)
docs.text:
• Client Decision: Archiving a project does not lock it into a read-only state. Users can still create new entries, edit/delete existing entries, and unarchive the project at any time.

  • Impact: Archiving is implemented as a UI/filtering state (status = 'ARCHIVED') rather than a backend permission lock. This is handled through PATCH /api/projects/:id/status.

docs.title: 3. Time Tracking, Live Timer & Overdue Flagging (US04)
docs.text:
• Client Decision:

  • Time tracking on logbook entries is mandatory.

  • The system must include a live timer feature for recording entry duration.

  • Entries/tasks must support flagging items as overdue.

  • Impact:

  • logbook_entries requires duration_minutes INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.

  • logbook_entries includes due_date TIMESTAMP to support overdue calculations.
  • logbook_entries includes entry_date TIMESTAMP to support backdating.
  • The frontend requires a live stopwatch/timer widget that calculates elapsed time.

docs.title: 4. Entry Editing & Account Erasure
docs.text:
• Client Decision: Logbook entries can be edited and deleted after creation. When an account is deleted, all user data, projects, and entries must be permanently erased.

  • Impact: Foreign keys enforce ON DELETE CASCADE where appropriate. This behaviour was verified in the Prisma schema.

docs.title: 5. Stats, Analytics & External API Integration
docs.text:
• Client Decision:

  • The system must include project statistics and analytics.

  • The external API integration should use a Calendar API, such as syncing logbook deadlines or entries to an external calendar.

  • Impact:

  • Backend provides GET /api/projects/:id/time-summary for per-project time aggregates.

  • The Dashboard provides cross-project statistics.
  • Calendar integration was identified as a future development requirement.

docs.title: 6. Entry Timestamps & Backdating
docs.text:
• Client Decision: The handling of entry timestamps was left to engineering discretion.

  • Engineering Decision: Include both created_at (system audit timestamp) and entry_date (user-customisable timestamp) on entries. This allows students to backdate work while maintaining an audit record.

docs.title: [Date: 2026-08-21] — Sprint Review & Rubric Compliance Check
docs.text:
• Channel: In-person sprint review meeting with client/lecturer.

  • Attendees: Client / Lecturer, Development Team (Dineo Motloung, Athandwa, Alondwe and Wendy).

docs.title: Meeting Context
docs.text: The client conducted a review of the project against the assessment rubric, checking the implementation status of the required features. The team presented the current state of the application, including authentication, project management, entry CRUD, time tracking, dashboard, profile, and settings.

docs.title: 1. Authentication — Confirmed as Core Requirement
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client confirmed that authentication, including user registration, login, email verification, and password reset, is an explicit rubric requirement and must not be treated as optional or deferred.

  • Status: Fully implemented — JWT-based authentication with registration, login, email verification, password reset, and account deletion.

  • Client Feedback: The client was satisfied with the implementation. Temporary development-mode auto-verification was considered acceptable during development, but production deployment should enforce real email verification.

docs.title: 2. Due Dates & Overdue Flagging — Non-Negotiable
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client reconfirmed that due dates and overdue flagging are mandatory requirements.

  • Decisions:

  • Every logbook entry must support a due_date field.

  • Entries past their due date must be automatically identified as overdue.
  • The UI must provide an Overdue section/filter alongside other entry views.

  • Overdue entries must be visually distinguished.

  • Impact:

  • logbook_entries.due_date is included in the Prisma schema.

  • Overdue status is determined using the entry due date and completion status.
  • The Entries and Project Detail views support overdue filtering.
  • The Dashboard includes overdue information.

docs.title: 3. Live Timer / Stopwatch for Time Tracking
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client emphasised that time tracking should go beyond manually entering a duration. A live stopwatch feature was identified as a required improvement.

  • Decisions:

  • The entry creation/edit form should include a live stopwatch.

  • The stopwatch should support start, pause, and reset.
  • The timer should measure elapsed time and convert it to the required duration value when saved.

  • Users should still be able to enter a duration manually.

  • Impact:

  • A stopwatch component was developed for the entry form.

  • Timer state is persisted during the active session to reduce the risk of losing timing information.
  • The existing duration_minutes backend field supports the saved duration.

docs.title: 4. Overdue Reminders & Notifications
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client asked about reminder capabilities for approaching deadlines.

  • Decisions:

  • The system should support advance reminders, such as reminders three days before, one day before, and on the due date.

  • In-app notifications are sufficient for the current implementation.

  • Email notifications are not required for the initial implementation.

  • Impact:

  • Deadline reminders were implemented in the application.

  • A notification indicator was added to provide users with visibility of notifications.
  • The existing due-date information is used to determine when reminders should be displayed.

docs.title: 5. Calendar API Integration (External API)
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client reconfirmed the requirement for an external API integration. The team proposed Calendar API synchronisation as the most natural integration for a digital logbook.

  • Decisions:

  • Logbook due dates should be exportable or synchronisable to an external calendar.

  • Google Calendar was identified as the preferred integration.

  • Calendar synchronisation was planned for a later development phase.

  • Impact:

  • The existing due_date field provides the required data for calendar events.

  • Google Calendar API integration requires OAuth2 configuration and external service credentials.
  • This feature remained planned at the time of the meeting. Since delivered: due dates sync to Google Calendar (FEAT-001).

docs.title: 6. Per-Project Time Recording with Stopwatch
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client asked about recording the total amount of time spent on individual projects.

  • Decisions:

  • Per-project total time should be calculated from the durations of the project's entries.

  • Time recorded using the stopwatch contributes to the relevant entry duration.

  • Project totals should be clearly visible to users.

  • Impact:

  • The existing GET /api/projects/:id/time-summary endpoint provides project-level time aggregation.

  • The Project Detail page can use this information to display cumulative project time.

docs.title: 7. Rubric Compliance Check
docs.text:
The client reviewed the following rubric areas:

  • Authentication & user management — Implemented (registration, login, email verification, password reset, and account deletion).
  • Project CRUD — Implemented (create, read, update, archive/unarchive, and unique name enforcement).
  • Customisable entry formats — Implemented with project-specific field definitions.
  • Entry CRUD with time tracking — Implemented with duration and due-date support.
  • Dashboard & statistics — Implemented with statistics and time summaries.
  • Data export/import — Implemented in Settings.
  • Dark mode / theme — Implemented with light, dark, and system themes.
  • Development setup guide — Implemented and maintained.
  • Testing — Integration tests implemented and passing.
  • Methodology documentation — Kanban board, user stories, and retrospective documentation maintained.

docs.title: [Date: August–September 2026] — Intermediate Development Follow-Up
docs.text:
The Intermediate phase involved significantly fewer formal client interactions than Sprint 1.

Most of the requirements for the Intermediate functionality had already been clarified during the previous in-person client/lecturer meetings, particularly the requirements discussed during the Sprint 1 review. Therefore, the team was able to continue implementation using the confirmed requirements without requiring another formal requirements meeting.

docs.title: Communication Channel
docs.text: • Channel: Team WhatsApp group used for occasional follow-up questions and clarification.

docs.title: Nature of Interaction
docs.text:
During the Intermediate phase, the team used the WhatsApp group to ask a small number of clarification questions when implementation details were unclear.

These interactions were primarily used to confirm interpretation of previously discussed requirements rather than introduce major new requirements.

The team therefore did not hold a separate formal client requirements meeting during this phase.

docs.title: Development Approach
docs.text:
The Intermediate user stories were implemented based on the requirements already established during the previous client meetings:

  • US07–US10: Rich field types, editable entry formats, format version preservation, and computed fields.
  • US11–US13: Custom-field statistics, alternative views, and unfinished-work/due-date functionality.
  • US14–US15: Offline capture, synchronisation, and data export/import.
  • Integration & Testing: Integration of the new functionality with the existing Basic features.

The team maintained the previously agreed Kanban methodology and continued using Gitea Issues, Projects, Labels, and Pull Requests to track implementation.

docs.title: 4. Intermediate Phase Outcomes
docs.text:
The Intermediate functionality was completed and integrated with the existing Basic Digital Logbook functionality.

The completed Intermediate functionality includes:

  • Richer custom field types.
  • Modification of existing entry formats.
  • Preservation of previous entry-format versions.
  • Computed fields.
  • Statistics and analysis of custom fields.
  • Alternative ways of viewing entries.
  • Unfinished-work and due-date tracking.
  • Offline entry capture and synchronisation.
  • Data export and import.

The implementation was tested together with the existing Sprint 1 functionality to identify cross-feature issues and regression problems.

docs.title: 5. Documentation & Deployment Update
docs.text:
During the Intermediate phase, the project documentation was also prepared for online access.

The MkDocs documentation site was successfully deployed using Netlify. The deployed documentation provides an accessible version of the project's technical and project-management documentation without requiring users to access local files.

A link to the deployed MkDocs documentation was added to the project's README.md so that team members, lecturers, and other reviewers can access the documentation directly from the Gitea repository.

The documentation deployment therefore replaced the previous plan of using Cloudflare Pages.

docs.title: 6. Current Outstanding Work
docs.text:
The following items remain as future improvements or later-phase functionality rather than unresolved requirements from the completed Intermediate user stories:

# Feature Status 1 Google Calendar API integration Done — due dates sync to Google Calendar (FEAT-001) 2 Further improvements to notification functionality Done — automatic reminders with push notifications (US28) 3 Further accessibility testing and WCAG improvements Future improvement (FEAT-006); a reduced-motion guard has been added 4 Additional automated unit tests for complex business logic Done — unit tests cover expressions, automation rules, computed fields and more

Statuses updated 2026-09-28.

The Intermediate user stories themselves have been completed and integrated into the project.

docs.title: [Date: 2026-09-18] — Client Meeting & Technical Feedback
docs.text:
• Channel: Client meeting.

  • Feedback:

  • The application is currently slow, so the team should investigate changing the deployment platform and deploy the application using Vercel.

  • The team should use MantisBT as the bug-tracking system to formally document and manage reported bugs.
  • The dashboard currently contains statistics that may be unnecessary because the application already has a separate statistics feature accessible through the side navigation. The team should consider removing the statistics section from the dashboard to avoid duplication.
  • The database was reviewed and it was identified that the tags table is missing. This is affecting the functionality of tags and preventing logbook entries from being updated correctly.
  • The missing tags table may also be contributing to the application's performance issues. The team should investigate possible glitches or delays in communication between the frontend and backend.
  • The team must properly document the internal APIs, including the available endpoints and their purpose, as required by the project.

  • The team needs to set up CI/CD so that testing and code coverage can be automated rather than relying on manually running tests and checking the coverage results.

  • Investigate and migrate the application deployment to Vercel to address the application's performance issues.

    • Status (2026-09-28). The deployment has not moved: the frontend is still on Cloudflare Pages and the backend on Render. The slowness was tackled in the code instead — see the performance item below.
  • Set up MantisBT and use it as the team's formal bug-tracking system.
    • Superseded (2026-09-25). The team chose a dedicated Gitea project instead; see the next meeting.
  • Remove the duplicated statistics section from the dashboard while keeping the dedicated statistics functionality accessible through the side navigation.
    • Done (2026-09-27). The dashboard's three statistics panels — Active Projects, Entries This Week and Total Time Logged — were removed, and the Statistics page in the side navigation is unchanged. The activity chart was kept: it shows the last seven days as working context rather than repeating a figure the Statistics page reports.
  • Add the missing tags table to the database and ensure that tags are correctly integrated with logbook entries.

  • Investigate and resolve possible frontend–backend communication glitches and performance issues.
    • Done (2026-09-28). Pages that sent one request per project now use a single request, the Entries page loads entries in pages, and database indexes were added for the common queries (US33).
  • Document the project's internal APIs, including endpoints, requests, responses, and their purpose.
    • Done. Every endpoint is documented in the API Reference.
  • Set up a CI/CD pipeline to automatically run tests and generate/check code coverage.
    • Done. Gitea Actions typechecks, lints, runs both test suites with coverage and posts the coverage on each commit. A passing push to main then deploys the API to Render and the frontend to Cloudflare Pages.

docs.title: 7. Summary
docs.text:
The majority of client requirements for the Intermediate phase were already established during the Sprint 1 client meetings. As a result, the team required only limited follow-up interaction during this phase.

Rather than creating artificial or unnecessary meetings, the team continued development using the requirements and architectural decisions previously confirmed by the client. Where clarification was required, questions were raised through the team's existing WhatsApp communication channel.

This approach allowed the team to continue development while maintaining a record of the decisions that informed the implementation.

The project documentation was also made accessible online through the deployed MkDocs site, with the documentation link included in the project README.

docs.title: 1.1 Methodology Used
docs.text:
We use a Kanban-based methodology with individual functional-area ownership rather than a traditional fixed-length Scrum sprint model.

The project is organised into functional areas, with user stories assigned to team members according to the relationships and dependencies between features.

For Sprint 1 – Core Logbook, the user stories were distributed as follows:

Team Member User Stories Functional Area Person 1 US00.1, US00.2, US00.3, US00.4 Authentication & Account Management Person 2 US01, US05 Project Management Person 3 US02, US03 Entry Structure & Entry Creation Person 4 US04, US06 Time Tracking & Entry Browsing

Work flows through a single shared Kanban board with columns:

Backlog → To Do → In Progress → Done

Each team member manages the flow of their assigned stories while coordinating with other members when cross-area dependencies arise.

For the Intermediate phase, work was divided into four functional areas:

Team Member User Stories Functional Area Person 1 US07, US08, US09, US10 Entry Formats & Fields Person 2 US11, US12, US13 Statistics & Views Person 3 US14, US15 Offline & Data Person 4 Integration & Testing Cross-feature Integration

For Sprint 3 – Advanced Logbook, work was again divided into four functional areas:

Team Member User Stories Functional Area Member 1 US22, US23, US24 Custom Statistics & Expressions Member 2 US25, US26, US27, US28 Personal Dashboard & Automation Member 3 US29, US30, US31, US32 Versioning & Record History Member 4 US33, US34, US35, US36, US37 Advanced Search & Performance

docs.title: 1.2 Reasoning & Motivation
docs.text:
• Why Kanban instead of Scrum: The project contains features with clear functional dependencies rather than work that must always be completed simultaneously within a fixed sprint. Kanban allows team members to progress their assigned functionality while making dependencies visible.

The core dependency chain established during Sprint 1 was:

Authentication → Projects → Entry Formats → Entries → Time Tracking / Browsing

The Intermediate phase builds on this foundation by extending entry formats and adding functionality that operates across existing logbook data:

Entry Formats → Rich Fields / Computed Fields → Statistics / Views → Offline / Data Portability

Sprint 3 operates on data whose shape the platform does not know in advance, so each area builds on the custom-field and entry model from the earlier phases. Its dependency chains were:

Custom Fields → Custom Expressions → Saved Statistics → Dashboard Panels → Dashboard Persistence

Entries → Version History → Historical Viewing → Restore Previous Version

Entries & Due Dates → Automation Rules / Recurring Entries → Automatic Reminders → Device Notifications

Custom Fields → Structured Search → Combined Filters → Result Ranking

Saved statistics (US23) had to exist before they could be offered as dashboard panels (US25), and version history (US29) had to record every change before a past state could be viewed (US30) or restored (US31). Archiving (US32) and long-term query performance (US33) apply across all of the above.

  • Functional Ownership: Related stories are assigned to the same developer where possible. For example, US07–US10 are closely related because they all extend the entry-format system, and US29–US31 all depend on the same version-history records. Keeping these stories together allows one developer to maintain consistency between related features.

  • Handling Cross-Area Dependencies: We use a status:blocked-on-dependency label. A story waiting on an upstream dependency remains in Backlog with this label. Once the required contract, schema, or functionality is available, the label is removed and the issue can move to To Do.

docs.title: 3.1 Sprint 1 – What Went Well
docs.text:
• Vertical slice delivery: All 10 core user stories from authentication through time tracking and entry browsing were implemented as end-to-end vertical slices covering the database, API, and UI.

  • Shared types package: Extracting types into @logbook/shared eliminated duplication and helped identify type mismatches between the frontend and backend early.

  • Integration testing: 27 Vitest tests running against the Neon database provided confidence that API endpoints worked correctly, including edge cases such as duplicate names, missing resources, and invalid input. The suite has since grown to 43 backend and 55 frontend test files.

  • Prisma ORM adoption: Migrating from raw SQL to Prisma simplified database access and provided type-safe queries.

  • Kanban workflow: The dependency-chain model worked well with functional ownership and made dependencies between areas visible to the team.

docs.title: 3.2 Intermediate Phase – What Went Well
docs.text:
• Feature ownership: Grouping related Intermediate stories by functional area helped maintain consistency between related features.

  • Extension of the existing system: The Intermediate features were developed on top of the Sprint 1 foundation rather than requiring a separate system.

  • Integration and testing: Dedicated integration work helped identify issues occurring between independently developed features and ensured that the new functionality continued to work with existing features.

  • Flexible entry model: Extending the entry-format system with richer fields and computed values moved the project closer to the specification's requirement for customisable logbook entries.

docs.title: 3.3 Sprint 3 – What Went Well
docs.text:
• Building on stored history: Because every save writes a version record, later features could rely on it. Automation rules record what they changed as their own version, so an automatic change can be seen and undone like a manual one.

  • Safe automation: Automation rules run only after an entry has been saved, cannot trigger themselves or each other, and skip a broken rule rather than failing the save, so a misconfigured rule never costs the user their entry.

  • Server-side persistence: Saving the dashboard layout on the server rather than in the browser means a student sees the same dashboard on every device.

docs.title: 3.4 What Could Be Improved
docs.text:
• Frontend error handling: The frontend uses basic error banners for API failures. A proper toast notification system would improve the user experience. Some failures are also reported misleadingly: when the backend cannot be reached, the login page reports "Invalid email or password."

  • Test isolation: Integration tests run against the live database without transaction rollback. Tests create and clean up data, but parallel test runs could potentially conflict.

  • Documentation gaps: Some documentation was written towards the end of development rather than incrementally. Future work should update documentation alongside implementation.

  • Cross-feature integration: As more Intermediate features were introduced, dependencies between features became more complex. Earlier integration of completed components would reduce the risk of discovering compatibility issues near the end of development.

  • Testing features that depend on deployment: Push notifications only work in a production build, and the hosted backend sleeps when idle on Render's free tier. Features like these need a deployed test environment, not only local development.

docs.title: 4. Remaining Improvements
docs.text:
Several improvements identified from client feedback after the Intermediate phase have since been delivered:

  • Unit tests now sit alongside integration tests for complex business logic, such as the expression evaluator and automation-rule conditions.
  • Google Calendar integration.
  • A live stopwatch in entry creation and editing.
  • Per-project cumulative time on the Project Detail page.
  • Deadline reminders with device notifications (US28).

Improvements that remain useful for further development:

  1. Use the toast notifications, so far shown only on the Open Work and Project Detail pages, for API errors across the app, and distinguish "server unreachable" from "wrong credentials" on the sign-in page.
  2. Improve the visual presentation of overdue entries.

These items are treated as future improvements rather than incomplete user stories.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Tool Version Notes Node.js v22+ Use nvm (recommended) npm v10+ Ships with Node.js nvm latest Optional, manages Node versions PostgreSQL — Hosted on Neon — no local install needed

docs.title: 1. Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://sdp.ms.wits.ac.za/no-boys-just-bugs/coms3011a-logbook-digital-logbook.git
cd coms3011a-logbook-digital-logbook

docs.title: 2. Set the Node version
docs.text: nvm use

docs.title: 3. Install dependencies
docs.text:
From the repository root (installs all workspace packages):

npm install

Then build the shared package once:

npm run build --workspace=packages/shared

@logbook/shared ships compiled JavaScript and declarations rather than TypeScript source, and the backend resolves it through packages/shared/dist. Until it is built, the backend fails to start with Cannot find module '…/node_modules/@logbook/shared/dist/index.js'. Re-run it after changing anything in packages/shared/src, or the backend keeps using the old build. (The frontend reads packages/shared/src directly through an alias in vite.config.ts, so it does not need the build.)

docs.title: 4. Configure environment variables
docs.text:
Create apps/backend/.env from the example file:

cp apps/backend/.env.example apps/backend/.env

Then edit apps/backend/.env. The example is a template, not working values: delete or blank every placeholder you are not replacing with a real value. A leftover placeholder such as RESEND_API_KEY=re_xxxxxxxxxxxxx makes the backend believe email is configured, so new accounts are no longer auto-verified and cannot sign in.

Required for local development:

Variable Purpose DATABASE_URL Neon connection string (Neon dashboard → Connection Details). Contains the database password. PORT Backend port, normally 3000 (the Vite proxy expects it). APP_URL Frontend URL, http://localhost:5173 locally. Used in email links and the Google Calendar redirect. JWT_SECRET Signs login tokens. Optional locally, but without it the backend generates a new secret on every start, so every restart signs you out. Required in production, where the server refuses to start without it.

Generate any secret in this guide with:

node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))"

Optional, per feature: leave these unset and the feature is simply off.

Variable(s) Feature Without it RESEND_API_KEY, RESEND_FROM Email via Resend (recommended) Accounts are auto-verified; links are logged to the backend console GMAIL_USER, GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD Email via Gmail SMTP (used only when Resend is not set) As above TWO_FACTOR_ENCRYPTION_KEY Encrypts 2FA secrets Enabling 2FA returns 503. Never change it once set: existing 2FA users would be locked out GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI, GOOGLE_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY Google Calendar sync The Calendar page reports that Google Calendar is not configured GEMINI_API_KEY (and optionally GEMINI_MODEL) The AI help assistant The assistant answers 503 and the chat says it is unavailable VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY, VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY (and optionally VAPID_SUBJECT) Push notifications for reminders (see Push notifications) Reminders stay in-app only; the backend logs VAPID keys not set on start RATE_LIMIT_*, RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED, TRUST_PROXY_HOPS Rate-limit tuning Sensible defaults apply; see the comments in .env.example

Warning: Never commit .env files with real credentials to the repository, and never paste real connection strings or keys into documentation — the docs site is publicly accessible. .env is already listed in .gitignore.

docs.title: 5. Set up the database schema
docs.text:
The backend uses Prisma 7 with a prisma.config.ts file that reads the DATABASE_URL from your .env. All Prisma commands must be run from inside the apps/backend/ directory:

cd apps/backend
npx prisma generate
npx prisma migrate deploy

The migration history was squashed on 2026-09-27 into a baseline, prisma/migrations/0_init, which creates the core schema (eighteen tables, enums, unique indexes and foreign keys) on an empty database. Dated migrations after it add the rest — push subscriptions, dashboard layouts, unique entry-field names, profile fields, My Grades, assessment reminders and saved filters — for twenty-three tables in all. npx prisma migrate deploy applies them in order, so it bootstraps a fresh Neon project end-to-end; there is no need for prisma db push, and new schema changes should arrive as dated migrations (npx prisma migrate dev --name <change>).

docs.title: 6. Run development servers
docs.text:
You need both servers running simultaneously:

Terminal 1 — Backend (Express API on port 3000):

npm run dev --workspace=backend

Terminal 2 — Frontend (Vite dev server on port 5173):

npm run dev --workspace=frontend

The frontend proxies /api/* requests to http://localhost:3000 via the Vite config.

Open http://localhost:5173 in your browser to use the app.

Note: Both servers must be running. Without the backend, the Vite terminal logs http proxy error: /api/… ECONNREFUSED and every request fails — see Troubleshooting.

When the backend starts you will see a SECURITY WARNING from pg about SSL modes. It is harmless; changing sslmode=require to sslmode=verify-full in DATABASE_URL silences it without changing behaviour.

docs.text: Command Location Description npm run dev apps/backend Start backend with hot reload (tsx watch) npm run build apps/backend Compile TypeScript to dist/ npm run start apps/backend Run the compiled backend (dist/index.js) npm run typecheck apps/backend Run tsc --noEmit npm run test apps/backend Run the Vitest suite (against the database in .env) npm run test:watch apps/backend Run tests in watch mode npm run test:coverage apps/backend Run tests with a coverage report npm run build packages/shared Compile the shared package to dist/ npm run dev apps/frontend Start Vite dev server npm run build apps/frontend Type-check and build the production bundle to dist/ npm run preview apps/frontend Serve the production build locally npm run test apps/frontend Run the Vitest + Testing Library suite (jsdom, no backend needed) npm run test:watch apps/frontend Run tests in watch mode npm run test:coverage apps/frontend Run tests with a coverage report npm run lint every workspace Run each workspace's linter (oxlint for the frontend, ESLint for the backend)

docs.title: Code Quality & Linting
docs.text:
The frontend uses oxlint for fast linting:

npm run lint --workspace=frontend

The backend uses ESLint with typescript-eslint:

npm run lint --workspace=backend

Every rule is an error except @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any, which is a warning on purpose: the backend handles untyped Prisma rows and raw SQL at a handful of boundaries, and failing every build over those would train the team to ignore the linter. The type checker still runs alongside it:

npm run typecheck --workspace=backend

Both linters run in CI on every push (see the pipeline below), so a rule violation fails the build rather than relying on someone remembering to run the command before pushing.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Both apps use Vitest.

  • Backend (apps/backend/src/__tests__/): integration tests using Supertest, one file per area (auth, entries, statistics, reminders, push, automation rules and so on). They run against the database in apps/backend/.env, so that file must be set up first.
  • Frontend (apps/frontend/src/**/__tests__/): component, page and library tests using Testing Library in jsdom. They mock the API and need no backend.
# Run all tests
npm run test --workspace=backend
npm run test --workspace=frontend

# Run one area only (matches file names)
npm run test --workspace=backend -- automation

# Run tests in watch mode
npm run test:watch --workspace=backend

See Testing for the test strategy.

docs.title: Shared Types Package
docs.text:
The @logbook/shared package (packages/shared/) contains TypeScript interfaces, Zod validation schemas, and types shared between frontend and backend. It is linked via npm workspaces ("@logbook/shared": "*").

After modifying shared types: 1. Rebuild the package: npm run build --workspace=packages/shared 2. Restart both dev servers

After changing apps/backend/prisma/schema.prisma, regenerate the Prisma client with npx prisma generate from apps/backend/.

docs.title: Authentication & Email
docs.text:
The app uses JWT-based authentication with email verification and optional two-factor authentication (2FA):

  • Registration creates a user with an unverified email
  • Email verification — a verification link is sent by email (if configured)
  • Login is blocked until the email is verified
  • Password reset — reset link sent via email
  • Two-factor authentication (2FA) — TOTP-based 2FA using otplib, with recovery codes. Users can enable/disable 2FA in Settings. When enabled, a QR code is generated for authenticator app setup. Requires TWO_FACTOR_ENCRYPTION_KEY.

Dev mode (no email provider): accounts are automatically verified so you can develop without email setup. The verification link is logged to the backend console.

Real email: set RESEND_API_KEY and RESEND_FROM (recommended), or GMAIL_USER and GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD. If both are set, Resend is used.

docs.title: Push notifications
docs.text:
Reminders can notify a device even when the logbook is closed, using web push.

  1. Generate a key pair once: npx web-push generate-vapid-keys.
  2. Put the pair in VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY and VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY — the same pair everywhere (local .env and the Render environment). A browser subscribed with one public key cannot receive pushes signed with another, and changing the keys cuts off every existing subscription.
  3. In the app, turn on Settings → Reminders → Notify me on this device and allow notifications when the browser asks. If it was already on before the keys were set, turn it off and on again.

Push only works in a production build. The service worker that receives pushes is registered only when import.meta.env.PROD is true, so under npm run dev the app falls back to in-app notifications: they appear only while a logbook tab is open, and the tab checks for due reminders every five minutes. Test real push against the deployed site, with the logbook tab closed but the browser still running.

If notifications never appear, check in order: the browser's site permission for notifications (Notification.permission in the console should be "granted"), the operating system's notification settings for the browser (including Do Not Disturb), and — on the deployed site — that the backend is awake, since Render's free tier sleeps when idle and pushes are only sent while it runs. On iPhone, push requires the app to be added to the home screen. Notification sound is controlled by the operating system, not the app.

docs.text: Part Host Address Frontend Cloudflare Pages https://coms3011a-logbook.pages.dev API Render (Docker, from the repository Dockerfile) https://digital-logbook-backend-latest.onrender.com/api Database Neon (PostgreSQL) DATABASE_URL in the Render environment Documentation Netlify (MkDocs) https://no-boys-just-bugs-digital-logbook-doc.netlify.app/

docs.title: The pipeline (CI/CD)
docs.text:
.gitea/workflows/deploy.yaml runs on every push to main and the team branches:

  1. CI — install, build the shared package, typecheck the backend, lint the backend and the frontend, run both test suites with coverage (the backend suite against a PostgreSQL database created for that run, both suites gated by coverage floors), report coverage on the commit, and build both apps.
  2. CD — on main only, and only after CI has passed:
    • the API is redeployed through a Render deploy hook;
    • the frontend is built and published to Cloudflare Pages with Wrangler;
    • the API's health check is called until it answers, so it is awake.

Each deploy step runs only once its secret exists, so the pipeline stays green until they are added. Repository settings → Actions → Secrets:

Secret or variable Where to get it RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL Render → the API service → Settings → Deploy Hook CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN Cloudflare → My Profile → API Tokens → a token with Cloudflare Pages: Edit CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID Cloudflare dashboard → Workers & Pages → the account ID in the sidebar CLOUDFLARE_PAGES_PROJECT (variable, not a secret) Cloudflare → Workers & Pages → the project's name; set it only if it differs from the default coms3011a-logbook

The backend suite gets a database of its own for each run. The DATABASE_URL secret is only its last-resort fallback, used (with a warning in the log) if the runner cannot start that database.

docs.title: Database migrations on deploy
docs.text:
The API container starts with npm run start:deploy, which runs prisma migrate deploy before serving. A deploy therefore brings the production schema up to date by itself; there is no separate migration step to forget. To apply migrations by hand instead:

cd apps/backend && DATABASE_URL=<production connection string> npx prisma migrate deploy

Neon's pooled endpoint can split a migration's advisory lock across connections, so a deploy's migrate deploy can then hang and time out (P1002). Production therefore also sets DIRECT_URL — the same database's direct endpoint, the host without -pooler — which prisma.config.ts prefers for the Prisma CLI. Leave it unset locally and in CI; DATABASE_URL is used instead.

docs.title: Keeping the API awake
docs.text:
Render's free tier sleeps after about 15 quiet minutes, and the first request then waits up to a minute (one cold start was measured at 33 s). To avoid that, a free cron-job.org job calls /api/health every ten minutes from 06:00 to 23:50 (Africa/Johannesburg). It runs on Wendy's cron-job.org account; ask there to change or pause it rather than adding a second pinger.

  • Why not the whole day: Render's free hours (about 750 a month) are shared by every free service in the workspace. Staying awake around the clock would use about 744; these hours use about 570, and a request at night still wakes the API, just slowly. Check the Render dashboard's usage page if another free service is added to the workspace.
  • Why not a Gitea schedule: .gitea/workflows/keep-warm.yaml used to do this, but 144 runs a day flooded the Actions tab, so it is now manual only. Run it by hand (Actions tab -> "Keep the API awake" -> Run workflow) before a demo or marking session at night, when the pinger is off.
  • What it looks like: the pings appear in Render's logs as GET /api/health every ten minutes. They read nothing and change nothing.

docs.text:
The project must stay above 50% combined coverage — that is the figure the marking rubric reads. Where it stands (2026-10-11, 1,616 tests):

Workspace % Lines Backend 85.16% Frontend 80.53% Combined 82.10% (6,819 of 8,306 lines)

The frontend is the lower of the two, so untested frontend code is what will trip a floor first — test the code you add. docs.title: Testing
docs.text: This page documents how the Digital Logbook is tested: our test stack and why we chose it, what is covered by automated tests, what we deliberately leave untested, the formal user feedback process, our testing policy, and proof of passing runs.

docs.title: Test Stack & Why We Chose It
docs.text:
Tool Role Why Vitest 4 Test runner and assertion framework Same engine that powers our frontend build tooling (Vite), so one dependency ecosystem covers the whole monorepo. Fast, ESM-native, and watch-mode works out of the box with TypeScript — no extra transpile config. Supertest HTTP-level request helper (backend) Lets tests call the Express app directly (request(app).post(...)) without starting a real server or opening a port. We test the real HTTP layer — routing, middleware, validation, status codes, JSON bodies — not just functions. React Testing Library Component testing (frontend) Tests components the way users interact with them — finding elements by placeholder text, role, and label rather than by implementation details like CSS class or component state. jsdom Browser environment for frontend tests Provides a lightweight DOM inside Node.js so React components can render, fire events, and validate forms without a real browser. The real Express app (src/app.ts) System under test (backend) The app module is exported separately from the server entry point (src/index.ts) precisely so tests can import it without binding port 3000. Real PostgreSQL Real database (backend) Integration tests run against a real PostgreSQL database — never a mock — exercising real Prisma queries, real constraints (unique, cascade deletes), and real SQL aggregation. CI provisions a throwaway database for every run, so the tests behave like production without writing into production data; the shared DATABASE_URL is only the last-resort fallback. Mocking Prisma would test our mocks, not our app. otplib TOTP code generation in tests The 2FA tests generate genuinely valid time-based codes with the same library the server uses to verify them, so the full TOTP round-trip is tested end-to-end.

Testing pyramid: the backend has integration tests (API-level, real database) and unit tests (pure functions); the frontend has component tests (rendered React components with jsdom) and unit tests (pure logic like saved-filter persistence).

docs.title: How the Tests Work
docs.text:
Backend API test — a real HTTP request to the real Express app backed by the real database:

it("PATCH /entries/:id/status marks entry DONE and sets completedAt", async () => {
  const res = await request(app)          // real Express app, no port
    .patch(`/api/entries/${statusEntryId}/status`)
    .set(H)                                // Authorization: Bearer <real JWT>
    .send({ status: "DONE" });

  expect(res.status).toBe(200);
  expect(res.body.status).toBe("DONE");
  expect(res.body.completedAt).not.toBeNull();
});

Frontend component test — renders the real React component in jsdom and asserts on DOM output:

it("renders the session-expired banner when the URL has ?expired=1", () => {
  window.history.pushState({}, "", "/login?expired=1");
  renderLoginPage();
  expect(screen.getByText(/session expired/i)).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Backend unit test — exercises pure functions directly:

it("verifyToken returns null for a tampered token", () => {
  const token = generateToken("user-1");
  const tampered = token.slice(0, -1) + (token.endsWith("A") ? "B" : "A");
  expect(verifyToken(tampered)).toBeNull();
});

Shared conventions across test files:

  • Own user per file (backend). Each suite creates its own test user (unique UUID + timestamped email), so suites never collide even though Vitest runs test files in parallel.
  • Setup in beforeAll, cleanup via cascade (backend). Fixed data is created once; afterAll deletes the test user and every foreign key is ON DELETE CASCADE.
  • Sequential within a suite where one test's output feeds the next (the 2FA lifecycle).
  • API modules mocked at the boundary (frontend). Frontend component tests mock ../api so they test the UI layer in isolation from the backend.
  • 60s per-test and hook timeout for backend tests — raised from 15s after a loaded CI runner measured a single test at 14.7s and a setup hook at 17s: a slow queue must not fail a run, while a genuine hang still does.

docs.title: How to Run Them
docs.text:
# Backend tests (from the repository root)
npm run test --workspace=apps/backend

# Frontend tests
npm run test --workspace=apps/frontend

# Watch mode (re-runs on file changes)
npm run test:watch --workspace=apps/backend
npm run test:watch --workspace=apps/frontend

Backend prerequisites: a reachable test database and a regenerated Prisma client (npx prisma generate in apps/backend — see Bugs Found By Testing).

Give the backend suite a database of its own locally. The suite creates and deletes its own users, projects and entries, so keep it away from your development data:

# once: an empty database next to your development one, with the schema
createdb logbook_test            # or CREATE DATABASE logbook_test;
(cd apps/backend && DATABASE_URL=postgresql://…/logbook_test npx prisma migrate deploy)

# each run: DATABASE_URL set for the command wins over apps/backend/.env
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://…/logbook_test npm run test --workspace=apps/backend

CI gives each run a PostgreSQL database of its own, with its schema built from the migrations, so the suite runs in under a minute and never writes into shared data. The workflow asks for a service container first; our Gitea runner does not provide one, so the step installs PostgreSQL inside the job instead. Only if both fail does the run fall back to the database in the DATABASE_URL repository secret, with fewer workers, and say so in a warning: over the network that database has made the suite take 12 to 20 minutes and fail on query timeouts. The log of the "Choose the test database" step says which one a run used.

Email behaviour in tests: with no SMTP credentials configured, registration auto-verifies (dev mode) and password-reset emails fail silently — both are caught and logged, and the endpoints still behave correctly. The tests assert the HTTP contract, never the email delivery.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
Workspace Lines Statements Branches Functions Backend 85.1% 84.2% 79.8% 92.6% Frontend 80.5% 78.9% 76.9% 76.4%

Measured 8 October 2026 with npm run test:coverage in each workspace. The largest remaining gaps are deliberate: the animated sign-in background (canvas drawing jsdom cannot render) and the parts of the project page exercised by the backend suite instead.

Coverage is measured with Vitest's V8 provider, configured in apps/backend/vitest.config.ts and in the test.coverage block of apps/frontend/vite.config.ts.

# Backend coverage (needs the same DATABASE_URL as the ordinary run)
npm run test:coverage --workspace=apps/backend

# Frontend coverage
npm run test:coverage --workspace=apps/frontend

Each run prints a summary table to the terminal and writes lcov.info to <workspace>/coverage/, which most editors and coverage viewers read directly. The coverage/ directories are gitignored; the numbers belong in CI output and in this document, not in the repository.

Both suites are configured with include: ["src/**"]. Vitest 4 removed the older coverage.all option, and without naming the sources explicitly a file that no test touches is simply absent from the report rather than counted as zero. Listing them keeps the percentage honest: it is coverage of the codebase, not coverage of the files that happen to have tests. Test files and the frontend's test-setup.ts and main.tsx are excluded, since measuring the tests against themselves says nothing.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
.gitea/workflows/deploy.yaml runs test:coverage rather than test for both workspaces on every push to main, master, Alondwe and Dineo. The text reporter puts the coverage table directly into the Actions log, so the numbers can be read from a run without downloading anything, and the two lcov.info files are uploaded as a coverage-lcov artifact.

The upload step is pinned to actions/upload-artifact@v3 and marked continue-on-error. Version 4 of that action depends on an artifact backend that not every Gitea runner provides, and a runner without artifact storage should not fail an otherwise green build — the coverage table is in the log regardless.

docs.title: Coverage on the commit
docs.text:
Gitea 1.24 has no built-in coverage display of the kind GitLab offers, so the workflow publishes the figure itself. .gitea/scripts/report-coverage.mjs reads the coverage-summary.json each workspace writes and posts three commit statuses through the Gitea API: coverage/backend, coverage/frontend and coverage/combined, each described as a line percentage and linking back to the run that produced it. They appear on the commit in the Gitea UI, so the number is visible per commit with no manual step.

The combined status is the one the marking rubric is judged on, which is why it is published rather than left for a reader to work out from the other two.

The script is Node rather than shell because jq and curl are not guaranteed on a self-hosted runner while Node is, setup-node having already run. It never fails the build: a missing summary, a missing token, a rejected request and an unreachable host are all logged and exited cleanly, and the step is additionally marked continue-on-error. Publishing a number is not worth turning a green run red.

It also appends the same table to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, which renders on the run page for runners that support summaries and is ignored by those that do not.

If the statuses do not appear, the log will say why — the likeliest cause is the runner's injected token lacking permission to write statuses, in which case a repository secret holding a token with write access can be passed to the step instead.

Coverage floors are enforced. After months of runs established the baseline, both configs grew a thresholds block: the backend fails below 80% of lines — the figure the final rubric asks about — and the frontend below 78%, deliberately a little under its current 80.5% because features land in that workspace faster than their tests, and a floor at exactly 80 would turn routine feature work red. Either way, a real regression fails the run instead of waiting for someone to re-read the report.

docs.title: The CI database link, and the ETIMEDOUT failures
docs.text:
The backend suites originally ran against the hosted Neon database over the public internet — now only the last-resort fallback (see the note under How to Run Them). On that path CI failed repeatedly with ETIMEDOUT — a transport error, raised before the statement ever reached Postgres — landing on an arbitrary query while everything around it read and wrote to the same database without trouble.

This section has now been wrong twice, so it records what was ruled out as carefully as what was tried.

Ruled out by measurement. Capping the worker count cut peak concurrency threefold and the failure did not move, which rules out connection-pool pressure. Other suites complete writes seconds before a failure in the same run, which rules out a cold start of the serverless compute.

Tried and did not work. The pool was created with a connection string and nothing else, so every pg.Pool default applied, including keepAlive: false. Enabling keepalive looked like the answer — DATABASE_URL points at Neon's -pooler endpoint, which drops connections that go quiet. It did not fix it: the next run went from three failures to eight. keepAlive is kept because it is right for a long-lived pool against a pooler, but it is not the cause. A speculative max: 5 added at the same time was removed again; it had no evidence behind it and the run got slower.

What the evidence actually showed. In the run of 2026-09-27 every one of the eight failures was a read that timed out: four in loadHistory's findFirst, three in the findUniqueOrThrow that takes the pre-edit snapshot in updateEntry, one in getEntries' findMany. Several surfaced not as an error but as a wrong answer downstream — an entry stuck at version 1, a time summary reading 30 instead of 90 — because the read failed inside a handler that carried on regardless.

The fix that follows from that. utils/readRetry.ts retries an operation only when both hold: it is one of the eight idempotent reads, and it failed with a transport code (ETIMEDOUT, ECONNRESET, ECONNREFUSED, EPIPE, or Prisma's P1001, P1002, P1017). Up to three attempts, with a growing pause. It is applied to every query through a Prisma client extension in prisma.ts.

Three things it deliberately never does: retry a write, because one that timed out at the transport may still have landed; retry raw SQL, because $queryRawUnsafe could be anything; and retry an error the database actually returned, so a constraint violation is still raised on the first attempt and cannot be hidden. readRetry.test.ts holds each of those as its own test.

This is also right beyond CI. A student should not see a 500 because one TCP connection went quiet between two of their queries, and a question asked twice returns the same answer.

The retry in entriesListing.test.ts predates this and is kept; its setup writes are idempotent by construction, since the user fixture upserts and the entry seed is guarded by a row count.

If ETIMEDOUT still reaches an assertion after this, the next thing to examine is load rather than connections: the suite runs for eight minutes against a free-tier instance, and automationEngine alone accounts for six of those.

docs.title: What We Don't Test (and Why)
docs.text:
No suite proves everything; these are the gaps we know about, stated so a reader knows exactly where the assurance of 1,616 green tests stops.

  • Full user journeys in a real browser. There are no end-to-end tests (Playwright/Cypress) driving the deployed app. Component tests render real pages and click real buttons, and the backend suite exercises every route they call, but nothing replays a whole journey — sign-in, then project, entry, statistics — against a running system. We judged the marginal assurance not worth a second test stack and its CI time.
  • The service worker, offline mode and push delivery, on a real device. The offline queue logic is unit-tested (offlineEntries, offlineProjects, offlineCache) and the push-subscription endpoints are integration-tested, but service-worker registration, background sync and notification delivery only truly happen in a browser jsdom does not simulate. Those paths are verified by hand, not by CI.
  • Live calls to third-party services. Google Calendar, the Gemini AI assistant and the email providers are mocked at the boundary. Real credentials would make the tests slow, non-deterministic, quota-bound and occasionally the sender of real email; the tests instead assert the behaviour around the boundary — request shaping, token refresh, error paths.
  • Performance under load. The API is rate-limited and queries are indexed, but no load test measures throughput or behaviour at concurrency. A query that degrades as data grows would not be caught.
  • Known thin spots inside the suites themselves, left visible in the coverage table rather than excluded from it: the two minute-ticker background jobs (jobs/recurringEntries.ts, jobs/pushReminders.ts, both 0% — thin setInterval wrappers around utilities that are tested), the recurring-entry utilities (41% of lines), the Google Calendar routes (29%), the email transport (66%) and the server entry point (index.ts, 0% — it only binds the port). On the frontend the largest gap is the animated sign-in background, drawn on a canvas jsdom cannot render.

Each is a deliberate trade-off for a course project on a free-tier CI runner; they are recorded so the judgement can be revisited rather than rediscovered.

docs.title: Testing Policy
docs.text:
1. Every API endpoint gets tests for the happy path and its error paths (400 validation, 401 auth, 404 missing, 409 conflict). If an endpoint has no error-path test, it isn't done.
  2. Never mock what we're testing at the integration level. No Prisma mocks, no stub auth. The database is real; failures must be real failures. Unit tests for pure functions may use mocks for external dependencies.
  3. Security behaviour is tested as behaviour, not implementation — e.g. we assert that unknown-email and wrong-password logins return byte-identical errors, not that some flag was set.
  4. Tests must clean up after themselves via user-cascade deletion, so the shared database stays usable.
  5. Regression rule: any bug found (see below) gets a test that would have caught it before the fix is considered done.
  6. Tests run in CI before every merge to main — a red suite blocks the merge. The Gitea Actions workflow runs both backend and frontend test suites on every push to protected branches.

docs.title: User Feedback Process
docs.text:
Automated testing checks what the code does; user feedback checks whether it works for real users. Our formal process:

  1. Instrument: a standard SUS (System Usability Scale) questionnaire — 10 fixed Likert items, scored 0–100 — so results are quantifiable and comparable across rounds.
  2. Scenario-based sessions: each tester gets the same set of task scenarios (register → create project → add entry → mark done → view stats/calendar → enable 2FA). We record pass/fail per task and where testers hesitate.
  3. Recruitment: 5–8 testers per round — classmates, other teams, and our client.
  4. Analysis & integration: SUS scores and task failures are reviewed as a team; each actionable finding becomes an issue on the tracker with an assigned fix, and fixed items are reported back in the next round.
  5. Records: each round is logged in docs/user-feedback.md with the raw scores, findings, and the feedback → action → commit trail.

Two rounds have been run: Round 1 on 14 September 2026 (Sprint 2, SUS 72.9) and Round 2 on 28 September 2026 (Sprint 3, SUS 72.5). The results are on the User Feedback page.
