docs.title: Bugs Found By Testing
docs.text:
Writing these tests surfaced two real issues — this is the regression rule in action:

  1. Stale Prisma client broke every entry-creation test (11 pre-existing failures). The generated client predated the Sprint 2 schema, so any query touching entry_fields.archived_at threw PrismaClientValidationError: Unknown argument archivedAt. Fix: run npx prisma generate after pulling schema changes. Lesson: prisma generate belongs in postinstall/CI.

  2. Concurrent entry-field creation can race on format versioning. Each field create does read-latest-version → insert latest+1. Two parallel creates both read version N and both try to insert N+1; the unique (project_id, version) constraint rejects one, so one field creation fails with 400. Fixed (BUG-001): the version bump now runs in a transaction and retries on a unique-constraint collision, so the loser of the race reads again and takes the next number. entryFieldIntegrity.test.ts creates and deletes fields concurrently and checks every version number is distinct and gapless.

docs.title: Future Work
docs.text: • Test isolation: CI now gives every backend run a PostgreSQL database of its own (with the DATABASE_URL secret kept only as a fallback), but the suites within one run still share that database and clean up after themselves via user-cascade deletion. A per-suite schema or transaction-rollback strategy would make it impossible for suites to observe each other's data at all.

docs.title: Completed
docs.text:
• CI gate — the Gitea Actions workflow runs both backend and frontend test suites on every push to main, master, Alondwe and Dineo. It needs a Gitea Actions runner to be online; while none is, runs wait in the queue and start once one returns.
  • Per-run test database — CI provisions a throwaway PostgreSQL for each backend run, so test data never lands in the production Neon database.
  • Coverage floors — the backend fails below 80% of lines and the frontend below 78%; a regression below the floor turns CI red rather than waiting for someone to re-read the report.
  • Backend linting in CI — ESLint runs on the backend alongside the frontend's oxlint; no-explicit-any is warn-only at the untyped Prisma/raw-SQL boundary, everything else is an error.
  • Backend unit tests — utils tests cover computedFields, auth, and entryFormat.
  • Frontend component and UI tests — page-level tests cover the dashboard, login/register, projects, entries timeline, open work, calendar, statistics and reminders pages, alongside the component and offline-layer suites.
  • Rate-limiting tests — rateLimit.test.ts locks in the BUG-003 fix.

Related: Third-Party Code documents the testing libraries and their licences, and Database Design describes the schema the integration tests run against.

docs.title: Third-Party Code
docs.text:
This page documents every third-party library and external service the Digital Logbook depends on, and — more importantly — why each one was chosen. Our policy is to lean on well-maintained, permissively licensed libraries for solved problems (authentication primitives, email, build tooling) while hand-writing everything that is core to the product (the REST API, business logic, database schema and UI components).

Every package below is declared in package.json (per workspace) and its license was verified from the installed package.json on disk.

docs.title: How we evaluate dependencies
docs.text:
Before adding a library we check:

  1. Fit — does it solve a problem we would otherwise hand-roll poorly (crypto, date handling, bundling)?
  2. Maintenance — is it actively maintained and widely adopted?
  3. License — permissive (MIT / BSD / Apache-2.0) so it is safe for a university project; no copyleft surprises.
  4. Size — is the dependency worth its footprint on the bundle?

docs.title: Backend runtime dependencies
docs.text: Package License What it does Why we chose it express ^5.2 MIT HTTP framework for the REST API Minimal and unopinionated — the course requires a hand-written API, and Express gives us routing/middleware without generating code or hiding the API behind heavy abstractions. v5 has native async error handling. @prisma/client ^7.9 Apache-2.0 Type-safe database access The generated client turns every query into TypeScript-checked code — schema drift becomes a compile error, not a runtime crash. Schema-as-code also gives us reviewable migrations. @prisma/adapter-pg ^7.9 Apache-2.0 Driver adapter for PostgreSQL Prisma's driver-adapter pattern lets us bring our own pg connection pool, which is the recommended way to talk to Neon's serverless Postgres over a pooled connection string. pg ^8.23 MIT PostgreSQL wire-protocol driver Required by the Prisma adapter; a mature, battle-tested driver. zod ^4.4 MIT Schema validation One validation library shared by frontend and backend through @logbook/shared — the same Zod schema validates the register form in React and the request body on the server. Single source of truth, no drift. jsonwebtoken ^9.0 MIT Signs and verifies JWTs Stateless auth: the server issues a signed token and verifies it on every request without a session store. The de-facto standard library for HS256 JWTs in Node. bcryptjs ^3.0 BSD-3-Clause Password hashing Pure-JavaScript bcrypt. We chose it over the native bcrypt package specifically because it needs no compilation — no node-gyp/native-module issues on teammates' Windows laptops. Same algorithm, identical hashes. otplib ^13.5 MIT TOTP two-factor authentication (RFC 6238) Implements the same standard that Google Authenticator / Authy use, so users can use any authenticator app. Actively maintained successor to speakeasy. qrcode ^1.5 MIT QR code generation Renders the otpauth:// provisioning URI as a QR data URL so users can scan it with their phone camera instead of typing a base32 secret. nodemailer ^9.0 MIT-0 Transactional email over SMTP Works with any SMTP provider — we send through Gmail with an app password — so there is no vendor lock-in and it works in local development without an API account. cors ^2.8 MIT Cross-Origin Resource Sharing middleware The frontend (Vite dev server on :5173, deployed frontend on Cloudflare Pages) calls the backend on a different origin; cors handles the preflight/OPTIONS dance correctly. dotenv ^17.4 BSD-2-Clause Loads .env into process.env Twelve-factor configuration: secrets (DB URL, JWT secret, Gmail credentials) stay out of the codebase. resend ^6.20 MIT Email API client Preferred email provider when RESEND_API_KEY is set; Gmail SMTP is the fallback. A REST API avoids SMTP ports that some hosts block. web-push ^3.6 MPL-2.0 Sends reminder push notifications Implements the standard Web Push protocol with VAPID keys, so the server can notify a student's devices directly through each browser's own push service — no third-party notification account or per-message cost. express-rate-limit ^8.7 MIT Rate limiting on the auth routes Caps sign-in, sign-up and 2FA attempts per IP to slow down password and code guessing (BUG-003). A small, standard Express middleware rather than a hand-rolled counter. googleapis ^181 Apache-2.0 Google Calendar API client and OAuth 2.0 Our external API integration: syncs entry due dates into the user's Google Calendar. Google's official client handles the OAuth code exchange and refreshes access tokens automatically.

docs.title: Licensing summary
docs.text: All dependencies use permissive licenses — MIT, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC, Apache-2.0 or MIT-0 — with one exception: web-push is under the Mozilla Public License 2.0. MPL-2.0 is a weak, file-level copyleft: it applies only to changes made to web-push's own files, which we use unmodified from npm. It places no obligations on our code, so the project's own licensing is unaffected. There is no GPL or AGPL code in the dependency tree.

docs.title: User Feedback
docs.text: This page documents the formal user feedback process we use to improve the Digital Logbook. Feedback is collected through a standardised instrument — the System Usability Scale (SUS) — combined with task-scenario observations and open-ended responses. Findings are tracked and every actionable change is recorded in the integration table at the bottom of this page.

docs.title: Why we collect feedback
docs.text: Automated tests verify that the code does what we intend; user feedback verifies that the product works for the people it's for. The feedback process is a required part of our methodology: every round of collection is followed by a round of integration, where each actionable finding becomes a tracked issue with an assigned fix.

docs.title: The formal process
docs.text: Stage What happens Instrument A Google Form with the 10 standard SUS items, round-specific self-report questions, and an open-ended prompt. Testers 5–8 per round: classmates, members of other teams, and our client (where available). Demographics are captured in the form itself. Session format 15–20 minutes, supervised. The tester works through the 7 task scenarios on the live app while an observer notes pass/fail and friction points on the observation sheet below. Recording Form responses land in a linked Google Sheet. An observer's written notes are kept alongside as a second data source. Analysis SUS scores per tester (0–100) and an average across the round; per-task pass/fail counts; open-ended responses grouped by theme. Integration Every actionable finding becomes an issue on the bug tracker with an owner and a fix commit. The integration table below records the full trail.

docs.title: The feedback form
docs.text:
Round 1 form: https://forms.gle/g4gEzYtiFRSXCQ5CA

Round 2 form (Sprint 3 revision): https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSenlkuuQC3bUS3WPXpBDO8M0O4eNDGurk669OKzzlunm0X_ow/viewform

The Round 1 form is structured in four sections:

  1. Welcome & About You — consent statement, role (Student / Lecturer or tutor / Working professional / Other), and prior experience with digital logbooks or work-tracking tools.
  2. Task Feedback — for each of 7 tasks (register, create project, add entry, mark done, view stats, view calendar/board, enable 2FA), the tester self-reports Completed easily / Completed with some difficulty / Could not complete, plus an optional comment field per task.
  3. System Usability Scale — the 10 standard SUS items on a 5-point Likert scale (Strongly disagree → Strongly agree). Worded verbatim; the SUS instrument is free to use and publicly cited across HCI research.
  4. Open Feedback — most frustrating part (required), favourite feature, one-thing-to-change, and an NPS-style 0–10 recommend-likelihood scale.

For Round 2 the questionnaire was revised so that every question maps to a criterion in the Sprint 3 rubric: the SUS instrument was kept intact (one 10-statement grid), and the task self-reports were replaced with feature-usage, save-correctness, load-speed, entry-field clarity, Calendar/Board discoverability, visual-integrity and one-thing-to-change questions.

A screenshot of the published form is captured after each round. The raw response data for each round is stored as a CSV file in this repository (docs/user-feedback-round1.csv and docs/user-feedback-round2.csv).

docs.text:
Self-reported answers are one half of the evidence; the other half is what the observer actually sees. For each session, fill in this table on paper alongside the tester:

Task Completed Notes / friction points 1. Register a new account ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 2. Log in and create a project with custom fields ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 3. Add a logbook entry (with duration + due date) ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 4. Mark an entry as done ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 5. Check project statistics (totals, averages) ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 6. Find calendar and board views ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 7. Enable two-factor authentication ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌

✅ = completed easily · ⚠️ = completed with difficulty · ❌ = could not complete.

docs.title: SUS scoring (in the linked Google Sheet)
docs.text:
When the form is linked to a Google Sheet (Responses → create spreadsheet), add these helper columns to auto-score each row:

Column Header Formula SUS_1 q1_adj =B2-1 (odd item: subtract 1) SUS_2 q2_adj =5-C2 (even item: 5 − answer) SUS_3 q3_adj =D2-1 SUS_4 q4_adj =5-E2 SUS_5 q5_adj =F2-1 SUS_6 q6_adj =5-G2 SUS_7 q7_adj =H2-1 SUS_8 q8_adj =5-I2 SUS_9 q9_adj =J2-1 SUS_10 q10_adj =5-K2 SUS score =SUM(q1_adj:q10_adj) * 2.5 (yields 0–100)

Adjust column letters to match the actual sheet columns produced by the grid question. The pattern — odd items score answer − 1, even items score 5 − answer, then sum and multiply by 2.5 — is the canonical SUS calculation from Brooke (1996).

Average SUS across the round: =AVERAGE(SUS_score_range). Industry benchmarks (Sauro, 2011) place the average SUS at 68/100; anything above ~72 is above-average, above ~80 is excellent.

docs.text:
• Login latency is the one recurring friction. Three testers named login or registration as the slowest moment, and nobody reported any other performance problem — consistent with the free hosting tier's cold start (see the integration table for what was done about it).
  • Reliability held up. Five of six testers saw no misbehaviour and reported that saving worked every time; the two exceptions were single occurrences with no reproduction detail.
  • Round 1's friction points did not resurface. No tester was confused by entry fields, and every tester found the Calendar and Board views straight away. The queued FEAT-002 / FEAT-003 improvements remain in the integration table.

docs.title: Integration: Feedback → Action → Commit

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook is designed as a non-monolithic web application consisting of a React frontend, an Express backend, and a PostgreSQL database.

The frontend communicates with the backend through a hand-written REST API. The backend handles business logic, authentication, validation, and database access.

This page explains the design decisions. For the system as built (deployment, folder layout, data model, API areas and background jobs), see System Architecture.

docs.title: Separation of Concerns
docs.text:
Layer Responsibility Technology Presentation UI rendering, user interaction, client-side routing, offline cache React 19, Tailwind CSS v4 API Request handling, authentication, validation, business logic Express 5, Zod, JWT Background work Recurring entries, reminder pushes, account purges Jobs in the API process Data Access Type-safe database queries, migrations Prisma ORM 7 Persistence Relational data storage PostgreSQL (Neon) Shared Common types and validation schemas @logbook/shared

The frontend never accesses the database directly. All data flows through the backend API, ensuring consistent validation and authentication enforcement.

docs.title: Authentication Flow
docs.text:
┌──────────┐    POST /api/auth/login        ┌──────────┐
│  Client  │  ───────────────────────────►  │ Backend  │
│  (React) │     email + password           │  bcrypt  │
│          │                                │  verify  │
│          │  ◄───────────────────────────  │          │
│          │  JWT, or "2FA required" +      │          │
│          │  5-minute pending token        │          │
│          │                                │          │
│          │    POST /api/auth/login/2fa    │  TOTP or │
│          │  ───────────────────────────►  │ recovery │
│          │  pending token + code          │  code    │
│          │  ◄───────────────────────────  │          │
│          │    JWT (7 days)                │          │
│          │                                │          │
│  Attach  │    GET /api/projects           │ require- │
│  token   │  ───────────────────────────►  │ Auth     │
│          │  ◄───────────────────────────  │          │
│          │    the user's own data         │          │
└──────────┘                                └──────────┘
  1. The user registers with email and password; the password is hashed with bcrypt before storage.
  2. A verification email is sent through Resend or Gmail SMTP. With no email provider configured (development), the account is verified automatically. Sign-in is refused until the email is verified.
  3. On sign-in, the password is checked. Without 2FA, a signed JWT valid for seven days is returned.
  4. With 2FA on, the backend instead returns a pending token that is valid for five minutes and good only for the second step. The client sends it with a code from the authenticator app, or a single-use recovery code, and receives the JWT. A code on its own is never enough to sign in.
  5. The frontend stores the JWT in localStorage and attaches it to every request through an Axios interceptor.
  6. The backend requireAuth middleware validates the token on protected routes.
  7. When a protected request returns 401 (the token expired or is invalid), the frontend clears the session and returns to /login?expired=1. A wrong password on a credential check is not treated as an expired session.

docs.title: Request Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
Every API request flows through the following pipeline:

Request → CORS → Body Parser → Rate Limit → Auth Middleware → Zod Validation → Ownership Check → Controller → Prisma → Response
  1. CORS: allows requests only from the frontend origins (localhost and *.pages.dev).
  2. Body Parser: parses JSON request bodies.
  3. Rate Limit: applies to /api/auth routes, with tighter limits on sign-in, sign-up and 2FA, to slow down password guessing.
  4. Auth Middleware: verifies the JWT and sets the user id (skipped for public routes).
  5. Zod Validation: validates the request body against its schema (400 on failure).
  6. Ownership Check: loads the project, entry, rule or statistic named in the path only if it belongs to the signed-in user. A resource owned by someone else is reported as not found (404), so its existence is not revealed.
  7. Controller: executes business logic.
  8. Prisma: performs type-safe database operations, in a transaction where several rows must change together.
  9. Response: returns JSON with the appropriate status code.

A valid token only proves who the caller is, not what they may touch, so the ownership check is a separate step on every route that names a resource.

docs.title: Shared Types
docs.text: Types and validation schemas that both sides need live in one package, @logbook/shared, so the frontend and backend cannot disagree about data shapes. The frontend reads the package's source directly. The backend uses its compiled output, so the package must be rebuilt after a change before the backend sees it. See System Architecture.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook uses a PostgreSQL database to store users, projects, project entry formats, logbook entries and their history, and the features built on top of them: tags, statistics, dashboards, automation, reminders, saved filters and the My Grades module tracker.

A key design goal was that different projects need different logbook entry structures (e.g. one project may track "hours worked" and "task completed", while another tracks "description" and "outcome"). Rather than hardcoding a fixed set of columns for logbook entries, we adopted an Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) pattern using ENTRY_FIELD and ENTRY_VALUE. This trades some query simplicity for the flexibility of letting each project define its own entry format without requiring schema changes.

We use UUIDs rather than auto-incrementing integers as primary keys to avoid exposing sequential, guessable IDs and to make it easier to merge or migrate data across environments without ID collisions.

The schema has twenty-three tables. The diagrams below split them into the core logbook, the features around it, and My Grades; USER, PROJECT, LOGBOOK_ENTRY and REMINDER appear in more than one.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• USER.email — Unique. Each email can only register once.
  • PROJECT(user_id, name) — Unique. A student cannot have two projects with the same name.
  • ENTRY_FIELD(project_id, lower(name)) — Unique among fields that are not archived, so a project cannot have two live fields whose names differ only in capitals. Statistics, expressions and automation rules refer to fields by name, so a duplicate would make them ambiguous.
  • ENTRY_VALUE(entry_id, field_id) — Unique. One value per field per entry.
  • ENTRY_FORMAT_VERSION(project_id, version) and ENTRY_VERSION(entry_id, version) — Unique. Version numbers increment per project and per entry.
  • TAG(user_id, name), CUSTOM_STATISTIC(project_id, name), AUTOMATION_RULE(project_id, name) — Unique names within their owner.
  • REMINDER(user_id, rule_key) — Unique, so a rule-generated reminder is created once however often the rules are applied.
  • PUSH_SUBSCRIPTION.endpoint — Unique. An endpoint belongs to one browser; if another user signs in on it, the subscription moves to them.
  • TWO_FACTOR_RECOVERY_CODE(user_id, code_hash) — Unique.
  • ACADEMIC_MODULE(user_id, code, academic_year) — Unique. Taking a module again in a later year is a new row, not a clash.
  • All foreign keys use ON DELETE CASCADE for full account erasure, except logbook_entries.format_version_id and logbook_entries.recurrence_rule_id, which use ON DELETE SET NULL — deleting a snapshot or a recurrence rule must not destroy entries.

docs.title: Indexes
docs.text: Besides the unique constraints above, the schema indexes the columns that common queries filter on: projects.user_id, entry_fields.project_id, logbook_entries by project_id, status, due_date and (project_id, status), entry_values by entry_id and field_id, entry_versions.entry_id, tags.user_id, and user_id on the recovery code, push subscription and Google Calendar tables. Reminders are indexed on (user_id, status, remind_at) for the due-reminder query, recurrence_rules on (enabled, next_occurrence) for the recurrence job, and automation_rules on (project_id, enabled) for the rule runner. saved_filters.user_id, academic_modules(user_id, academic_year), assessments.module_id and reminders.assessment_id are indexed for the saved-filter, My Grades and assessment-reminder lookups.

docs.title: User
docs.text:
Represents a student using the Digital Logbook.

A user can have multiple projects and can request multiple password resets over time.

Passwords are stored as a salted hash (password_hash), never as plain text.

Authentication-related columns:

  • is_email_verified, email_verification_token, email_verification_expiry — email ownership is proven before login is allowed. The token is 32 random bytes, expires after one hour, and only its SHA-256 digest is stored.
  • two_factor_secret, is_two_factor_enabled — optional TOTP two-factor authentication. The secret is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before storage. It is staged at setup time and only becomes active (is_two_factor_enabled = true) after the user proves their authenticator works.
  • scheduled_deletion_at — set when the user deletes their account. The account stays usable for a 30-day grace period and is erased by the hourly purge job, or at the next sign-in attempt, once this date has passed.

See apps/backend/AUTHENTICATION.md in the repository for the full authentication design.

docs.title: Two-Factor Recovery Code
docs.text: One of ten single-use codes issued when 2FA is enabled, for signing in without the authenticator device. Only a digest is stored; used_at is set when a code is spent. Regenerating the codes replaces the whole set.

docs.title: Project
docs.text:
Represents a separate project belonging to a student.

A project can contain multiple entry fields, format versions, and logbook entries. Archiving sets status = ARCHIVED; entries stay editable either way.

docs.title: Entry Field
docs.text:
Defines the structure of a project's logbook entries.

For example, a project could define fields such as:

  • Description (TEXT)
  • Date (DATE)
  • Hours worked (NUMBER)
  • Task completed (BOOLEAN)

type is enforced at the application layer when validating ENTRY_VALUE.value, since the value itself is stored as a string to support different field types.

Sprint 2 extended the field types beyond the basic four:

Type Meaning TAGS A list of short labels CHECKLIST A list of checkable items LINK A web address (http or https) REFERENCE A reference to another project or entry COMPUTED A value derived from other fields via formula rather than typed in

archived_at implements soft retirement: a field dropped from the format stops appearing on new entry forms, but existing values remain readable in old entries. formula is only populated for COMPUTED fields and stores the expression the server evaluates on save.

docs.title: Entry Format Version
docs.text:
An immutable snapshot of a project's entry format, taken whenever the format changes (field added, dropped, renamed, or re-typed).

This is what keeps historical entries readable: each entry pins the format version that was current when it was created (format_version_id), so later format changes never break old entries. Changing a format creates a new snapshot and carries existing entries forward — filling in what it reasonably can — rather than abandoning them.

The snapshot itself is stored as JSONB (fields), which keeps the whole field definition set together and queryable.

docs.title: Logbook Entry
docs.text:
Represents a recorded activity within a project.

An entry stores the date it was recorded (entry_date, user-editable for backdating), the amount of time spent (duration_minutes), an optional deadline (due_date), and its completion state:

  • status — OPEN (work still to do) or DONE.
  • completed_at — timestamp set when the entry is marked done.
  • archived_at — set when the entry is moved to the archive. Archived entries are left out of the default views but not deleted.
  • recurrence_rule_id — the rule that generated the entry, if it recurs.

Open entries with past due dates surface automatically in the Overdue view and the Open Work page's due-date buckets.

docs.title: Entry Value
docs.text:
Stores the value entered for a particular field of a particular logbook entry.

This allows different projects to have different entry structures.

docs.title: Entry Version
docs.text: The history of an entry. A row is written on every create, edit, status change, restore and automated change, and rows are never updated or deleted, so a correction always keeps what it replaced. snapshot holds the whole entry as the API returned it at that moment, field names included, so an old version still reads correctly after the project's fields are renamed or removed. Viewing an entry "as of" a date reads the newest version at or before it; restoring writes a new RESTORED version rather than rewriting history.

docs.title: Password Reset
docs.text: Stores a password-reset request for a user. Each record contains a unique, time-limited token sent to the user's email, and an expires_at timestamp so that reset links become invalid after a short period. Tokens are single-use: all of a user's reset records are deleted in the same transaction that updates the password. Only a SHA-256 digest of the token is stored, never the token itself. This supports the US00.3 – Reset Password user story defined in the Development Plan.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: TAG is a user's own vocabulary of labels, applied to projects through PROJECT_TAG and to entries through ENTRY_TAG. Tags are independent of the per-project entry format, so they work the same on every project.

docs.title: Custom Statistic
docs.text: US23. A named expression over a project's entries. Only the definition is stored: the value is worked out on every read, so it follows the data instead of freezing the number it had when it was saved.

docs.title: Dashboard Layout
docs.text: US26. The panels a user chose for their dashboard, in the order they arranged them, one row per user. Keeping it on the server rather than in the browser means the same dashboard appears on every device.

docs.title: Automation Rule
docs.text:
US24. A rule that watches one project's entries and applies an action — add a tag, remove a tag, or set the entry's status — when its conditions hold. Rules are evaluated when an entry is captured or updated, after the save commits, so a broken rule can never cost the user their work.

conditions and action are stored as JSONB rather than normalised tables: a rule is read whole, written whole, and never queried by its parts, so splitting it would add joins without adding a query. user_id sits alongside project_id (as it does for custom_statistics) — it is redundant, since a project has one owner, but it keeps ownership checks single-column. The @@index(project_id, enabled) is the only index an entry save needs: the runner reads a project's enabled rules and evaluates them in memory against the entry it just loaded. See the "Automation Rules" section of the API reference for the rule language and its deliberate limitations.

docs.title: Recurrence Rule
docs.text: US27. A stable template for an entry that repeats daily, weekly or monthly. Each occurrence is generated from the template rather than copied from the previous occurrence, so editing or completing one occurrence does not change the pattern. next_occurrence is when the next entry is due; the recurrence job and entry reads both create any that have fallen due.

docs.title: Reminders
docs.text: US28. A REMINDER is either set by the user (MANUAL) or generated from the user's REMINDER_SETTINGS: entries due soon, overdue entries, entries left untouched for a while (STALE), and a daily prompt when nothing has been logged. rule_key identifies which rule and entry produced a generated reminder, so it is only created once. pushed_at records that the reminder has been sent to the user's devices, so it is never pushed twice. PUSH_SUBSCRIPTION holds one row per browser the user has allowed to receive notifications.

docs.title: Google Calendar Connection
docs.text: The user's Google OAuth tokens, encrypted at rest, used to mirror entry due dates into their calendar. At most one per user.

docs.title: Profile
docs.text: The profile card lives on USER itself: bio, avatar (a downscaled image stored as a data URL), student_number, degree and year_of_study. All are optional, and keeping them on the server means the profile follows the student between devices.

docs.title: Saved Filter
docs.text: A named combination of Entries page filters (search text, project, tab, sort, tags, custom-field filters and archive state), stored as JSONB because it is read and written whole. Kept on the account so saved filters follow the student between devices; the browser keeps a copy for offline use.

docs.title: Academic Module and Assessment
docs.text: The My Grades extra feature (FEAT-009). An ACADEMIC_MODULE is a course the student takes in a given year, either one semester or the full year; an ASSESSMENT is one weighted piece of work in it. A mark is kept as entered, out of a maximum or as a percentage, and missed counts as 0% while staying distinct from an entered zero. A dated assessment with remind on generates ASSESSMENT reminders 5 and 2 days before its date; they are deleted with it.

docs.title: How changes are applied
docs.text: The schema is managed with Prisma Migrate. On 2026-09-27 the accumulated migration history was squashed into a single baseline, prisma/migrations/0_init/migration.sql, generated with prisma migrate diff --from-empty --to-schema prisma/schema.prisma --script and verified to reproduce the live schema at that time (a drift diff reported no differences, and deploying it to an empty database created every table). npx prisma migrate deploy applies the baseline and every dated migration after it, so it bootstraps a fresh environment end-to-end. New schema changes are made by editing schema.prisma and running npx prisma migrate dev --name <change>, which adds a dated migration on top of the baseline. The incremental migrations that the baseline replaced remain visible in the git history.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: The database is a managed PostgreSQL instance hosted on Neon (serverless, autoscaling). The backend connects with Prisma's driver adapter using the DATABASE_URL environment variable; connection strings never leave the environment configuration.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Development of the Digital Logbook follows a structured, dependency-driven approach. User stories are implemented in groups based on the functionality they provide and the dependencies between them.

The development sequence began with authentication and account management, followed by project management, entry format configuration, logbook entry creation, entry browsing, and integration and testing. The Intermediate phase extended the Basic functionality with richer field types, entry-format versioning, computed fields, custom-field analysis, alternative views, unfinished-work tracking, offline capture, and data export/import. The Advanced phase (Sprint 3) added owner-defined statistics, a personal dashboard, automation, a full record history, and search and performance work for long-lived logbooks.

Development was carried out incrementally, with each phase producing functionality that could be integrated with the functionality developed in previous phases.

docs.title: Development Approach
docs.text:
Development was carried out incrementally using the following principles:

  • Implement foundational functionality before dependent functionality.
  • Develop related user stories together where they share functionality.
  • Use the database design and system architecture as the basis for implementation.
  • Test functionality against its user-story acceptance criteria.
  • Integrate frontend, backend, and database components throughout development.
  • Preserve existing project and entry data when implementing operations such as project archiving.
  • Extend existing functionality rather than unnecessarily duplicating functionality.
  • Test new Intermediate functionality together with the existing Basic functionality to identify integration and regression issues.
  • Record every change to an entry, so that later features (history, restore, automation) can rely on it and no correction loses data.

The project continued to use the Gitea Kanban board, Issues, Labels, Milestones, branches, and pull requests to track development.

docs.title: Development Sequence
docs.text:
The overall development sequence was:

flowchart LR

    A["Phase 1<br/>Authentication"] --> B["Phase 2<br/>Project Management"]

    B --> C["Phase 3<br/>Entry Format Configuration"]

    C --> D["Phase 4<br/>Logbook Entries & Time"]

    D --> E["Phase 5<br/>Entry Browsing & Filtering"]

    E --> F["Phase 6<br/>Integration & Testing"]

    F --> G["Phase 7<br/>Intermediate Features"]

    G --> H["Phase 8<br/>Intermediate Integration & Testing"]

    H --> I["Phase 9<br/>Advanced Features (Sprint 3)"]

    I --> J["Phase 10<br/>Advanced Integration & Testing"]

The sequence reflects the dependencies between the user stories. For example, a project must exist before an entry format can be defined for it, and an entry format must exist before a project-specific logbook entry can be created.

The Intermediate phase builds on the completed Basic functionality rather than replacing it, and the Advanced phase builds on both.

docs.title: User Stories
docs.text:
• US00.1 – Create an Account
  • US00.2 – Sign In
  • US00.3 – Reset Password
  • US00.4 – Delete Account

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text:
This phase established the account and authentication functionality required to associate logbook data with individual students.

Development included:

  • Creating the account registration interface.
  • Validating registration information.
  • Preventing duplicate accounts.
  • Implementing secure authentication.
  • Associating authenticated users with their projects and entries.
  • Implementing password-reset functionality.
  • Implementing account deletion and the required data-deletion behaviour.
  • Protecting authenticated application functionality from unauthorised access.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: US00.1 and US00.2 formed the foundation for the remaining authentication functionality. Password reset and account deletion depend on the account and authentication infrastructure.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A student can create an account, sign in, reset their password, and delete their account.

docs.title: User Stories
docs.text:
• US01 – Create a Project
  • US05 – Archive a Project

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text:
This phase introduced project management functionality.

Development included:

  • Creating projects with a name and optional description.
  • Associating projects with the authenticated student.
  • Displaying projects in the student's project list.
  • Setting newly created projects as active.
  • Implementing project archiving.
  • Separating active and archived projects in the interface.
  • Ensuring that archiving a project does not delete its entries or historical data.
  • Supporting project unarchiving.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Projects depend on authentication because each project belongs to a student.

US05 extends the project functionality implemented for US01.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A student can create and manage projects, archive completed projects, and retain access to their historical project information.

docs.title: User Story
docs.text: • US02 – Define a Project's Entry Format

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text:
This phase implemented the custom entry structure for each project.

Development included:

  • Providing an interface for defining entry fields.
  • Allowing students to add fields to a project.
  • Allowing field names to be specified.
  • Allowing the value type of each field to be selected.
  • Associating entry fields with their project.
  • Persisting entry-format definitions in the database.
  • Ensuring that different projects can have different entry formats.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
US02 depends on US01 because an entry format must be associated with an existing project.

The resulting entry format is a direct dependency for US03 because the entry creation form uses the fields defined for the selected project.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A student can configure a custom entry format for each project.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Logbook Entry Creation and Time Tracking
User Stories
docs.text:
• US03 – Record a Logbook Entry
  • US04 – Record Time Spent on an Entry

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text:
This phase implemented the core logbook functionality.

Development included:

  • Allowing the student to select a project when creating an entry.
  • Dynamically displaying the fields defined by that project's entry format.
  • Validating entered field values.
  • Saving logbook entries to the database.
  • Recording entry dates and creation information.
  • Associating each entry with the selected project.
  • Allowing students to record time spent on an activity.
  • Persisting recorded time with the entry.
  • Supporting live time tracking.
  • Supporting due dates and overdue identification.
  • Calculating or updating project-level recorded time.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
US03 depends on US01 and US02 because an entry requires an existing project and its entry format.

US04 extends US03 because time spent is recorded as part of a logbook entry.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A student can create project-specific logbook entries using the configured entry format and record the time spent on each entry.

docs.title: User Story
docs.text: • US06 – Browse and Filter My Entries

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text:
This phase provided functionality for reviewing recorded work.

Development included:

  • Displaying the student's logbook entries.
  • Ordering entries chronologically.
  • Displaying the project associated with each entry.
  • Allowing entries to be filtered by project.
  • Providing an entry detail view.
  • Supporting identification of overdue entries.
  • Ensuring that filtering only changes how entries are displayed and does not modify stored data.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: US06 depends on the existence of logbook entries created through US03.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A student can browse their recorded entries, filter them by project, and view individual entry information.

docs.title: Phase 6 — Basic Integration, Testing and Refinement
Development Work
docs.text:
This phase focused on integrating the Basic functionality into a complete application and verifying that the system satisfied the requirements.

Development included:

  • Integrating frontend, backend, and database functionality.
  • Testing API interactions between the frontend and backend.
  • Testing database relationships and data persistence.
  • Testing authentication and access control.
  • Testing user stories against their acceptance criteria.
  • Testing interactions between projects, entry formats, and logbook entries.
  • Testing project archiving without loss of historical data.
  • Validating form input and handling invalid data.
  • Handling application and API errors.
  • Testing responsive layouts and common user interactions.
  • Fixing defects identified during testing.
  • Performing usability and consistency checks.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: An integrated Basic Digital Logbook supporting authentication, project management, custom entry formats, logbook entries, time tracking, and entry browsing.

docs.title: Phase 7 — Intermediate Functionality
docs.text: The Intermediate phase extended the Basic Digital Logbook with additional customisation, analysis, organisation, offline, and data-management functionality.

docs.title: User Stories
docs.text:
• US07 – Rich Field Types
  • US08 – Modify Existing Entry Format
  • US09 – Preserve Previous Entry Format Versions
  • US10 – Computed Fields
  • US11 – Analyse Custom Fields
  • US12 – Alternative Views
  • US13 – Unfinished Work and Due Dates
  • US14 – Capture Entries Offline
  • US15 – Export and Import Logbook Data

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text: Development included the following functionality.

docs.title: US07 — Rich Field Types
docs.text:
The entry-format functionality was extended to support richer types of custom fields beyond the original basic field configuration.

This allows project entry formats to better represent the type of information students need to record.

docs.title: US08 — Modify Existing Entry Format
docs.text:
Existing project entry formats can be modified after they have been created.

The entry-format interface was extended to support changes to the structure of project entries while maintaining the relationship between projects and their entry formats.

docs.title: US09 — Preserve Previous Entry Format Versions
docs.text:
Entry-format changes were implemented with consideration for previously recorded entries.

Previous format information is preserved so that modifying the format does not unnecessarily invalidate historical logbook data.

docs.title: US10 — Computed Fields
docs.text:
Computed fields were introduced to allow supported fields to derive values from other entry information.

This extends the entry format from a purely data-capture structure into a structure that can also provide calculated information.

docs.title: US11 — Analyse Custom Fields
docs.text:
The application was extended to provide statistics and analysis based on custom entry fields.

This provides students with additional ways to understand information recorded in their logbook rather than only displaying individual entries.

docs.title: US12 — Alternative Views
docs.text:
Alternative ways of viewing entries were introduced to make recorded work easier to organise and review.

These views complement the existing chronological and project-filtered entry browsing functionality.

docs.title: US13 — Unfinished Work and Due Dates
docs.text:
The application supports tracking unfinished work and due dates.

Development included functionality for identifying work that has not been completed and distinguishing entries based on their deadline status.

This builds on the due-date functionality established during the Basic development.

docs.title: US14 — Capture Entries Offline
docs.text:
Offline capture functionality was introduced so that students can record logbook information when a connection is temporarily unavailable.

Offline information can be retained and synchronised when connectivity becomes available.

docs.title: US15 — Export and Import Logbook Data
docs.text:
The application supports exporting and importing logbook data.

This provides students with a way to retain, transfer, or restore their logbook information without directly accessing the database.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
The Intermediate functionality builds on the Basic functionality.

The main dependencies are:

  • US07 depends on the existing custom entry-format functionality from US02.
  • US08 and US09 depend on the existing entry-format and entry data structures.
  • US10 depends on the custom field structure and entry data.
  • US11 depends on stored custom-field and entry data.
  • US12 and US13 extend the existing entry browsing and due-date functionality.
  • US14 extends the existing entry-creation functionality.
  • US15 operates on the existing project and entry data.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: The Digital Logbook supports the completed Intermediate functionality while retaining the Basic functionality developed previously.

docs.title: Phase 8 — Intermediate Integration, Testing and Refinement
Development Work
docs.text:
The final Intermediate phase focused on integrating the additional functionality with the existing application.

Development and testing included:

  • Integrating Intermediate frontend functionality with the existing application.
  • Integrating Intermediate backend functionality with the existing database structure.
  • Testing interactions between Basic and Intermediate features.
  • Testing modified entry formats with existing project and entry data.
  • Testing alternative entry views.
  • Testing unfinished and overdue work.
  • Testing offline capture and synchronisation.
  • Testing export and import functionality.
  • Testing custom-field analysis and computed fields.
  • Testing validation and error handling.
  • Performing regression testing against previously implemented functionality.
  • Fixing integration defects identified during development.
  • Reviewing the consistency of the user interface across the expanded application.

docs.title: Documentation and Deployment
docs.text:
The project documentation was also made available online during this phase.

The MkDocs documentation site was deployed using Netlify, and a link to the deployed documentation was added to the project's README.md.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A fully integrated Digital Logbook containing the Basic and Intermediate functionality, supported by project documentation and testing.

docs.title: Phase 9 — Advanced Functionality
docs.text: The Advanced phase answers the brief's request for a logbook that computes over data whose shape only its owner knows, keeps its record hard to lose, does some of the writing itself, and stays quick after years of use. The sixteen stories were tracked as Gitea issues #94–#109 under the Sprint 3 - Advanced Logbook milestone and divided into four functional areas.

docs.title: User Stories
docs.text: Area Stories Board status Custom Statistics & Expressions US22 Define Custom Expressions, US23 Save Custom Statistics, US24 Entry Automation Rules Done Personal Dashboard & Automation US25 Create a Custom Dashboard, US26 Arrange and Persist Dashboard Layout, US27 Create Recurring Entries, US28 Generate Automatic Reminders Done Versioning & Record History US29 Preserve Entry Version History, US30 View an Entry as It Existed on a Given Date, US31 Restore a Previous Entry Version, US32 Archive Old Entries Done Advanced Search & Performance US33 Maintain Query Performance for Large Logbooks, US34 Apply Rules When Capturing Entries (same story as US24), US35 Rank Search Results by Relevance, US36 Combine Search Filters, US37 Search Custom Fields Done

docs.title: Custom Statistics & Expressions
docs.text:
US22 — Define Custom Expressions. A student writes an expression such as SUM({Hours}) / COUNT() over a project's entries. The server parses and evaluates it itself; no user input is ever executed, and field names reach the database only as bound parameters after being matched against the project's own fields.

US23 — Save Custom Statistics. An expression can be saved with a name and appears alongside the built-in statistics. Only the definition is stored, so the value always reflects the current entries.

US24 — Entry Automation Rules. A rule watches a project's entries and adds or removes a tag or sets the status when its conditions hold. Rules run after the entry is saved, cannot trigger themselves or each other, and a broken rule is skipped rather than failing the save.

docs.title: Personal Dashboard & Automation
docs.text:
US25 — Create a Custom Dashboard. The student chooses which statistics and information panels to show, including their saved statistics.

US26 — Arrange and Persist Dashboard Layout. The chosen panels and their order are stored on the server, so the same dashboard appears on every device.

US27 — Create Recurring Entries. An entry can repeat daily, weekly or monthly. Occurrences are generated from a stored template, both by a background job and when entries are read, so none are missed while the server sleeps.

US28 — Generate Automatic Reminders. Reminders are raised for entries due soon, overdue entries, entries left untouched, and a daily prompt when nothing has been logged, alongside reminders the student sets by hand. They are delivered as web push notifications when the logbook is closed.

docs.title: Versioning & Record History
docs.text:
US29 — Preserve Entry Version History. Every create, edit, status change, restore and automated change writes an immutable snapshot of the entry.

US30 — View an Entry as It Existed on a Given Date. The newest version at or before a chosen date is shown.

US31 — Restore a Previous Entry Version. An earlier version becomes current again. The restore is itself saved as a new version, so nothing is lost by restoring.

US32 — Archive Old Entries. Old entries move to an archive that keeps them but leaves them out of the default views.

docs.title: Advanced Search & Performance
docs.text:
US33 — Maintain Query Performance for Large Logbooks. Database indexes on the columns common queries filter by, a paginated Entries page, and a single request for open work instead of one per project.

US34 — Apply Rules When Capturing Entries. Overlaps with US24, whose rule engine already applies rules when an entry is captured.

US35–US37 — Search. Searching inside specific custom fields, combining several filters in one search, and ranking results by relevance rather than by date.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• US22 depends on the custom fields and entry values from US02, US03 and US10.
  • US23 depends on US22, and US25 depends on US23 to offer saved statistics as panels. US26 extends US25.
  • US24 depends on the entry-save path from US03 and on tags; its changes are recorded through US29.
  • US27 depends on entry creation (US03); US28 depends on due dates (US13) and entry status.
  • US30 and US31 depend on the version history from US29.
  • US32 and US33 apply across all entry features; US35–US37 depend on custom fields (US02) and the existing browsing and filtering (US06).

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A logbook whose owner can compute over their own data, arrange their own dashboard, have entries and reminders generated for them, and see and restore any past state of an entry.

docs.title: Phase 10 — Advanced Integration, Testing and Refinement
Development Work
docs.text:
• Testing each Advanced story against its acceptance tests with backend integration tests and frontend tests.
  • Testing that automation, recurrence and restores all write version history.
  • Testing ownership: one student's statistics, rules, reminders, layouts and history cannot be read or changed by another.
  • Testing that a broken automation rule or an unreadable statistic never costs the user an entry or a whole page.
  • Testing push notifications against a production build, since the service worker is only registered there.
  • Regression testing against the Basic and Intermediate functionality.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: The Advanced functionality integrated with the existing Digital Logbook, with all Sprint 3 stories complete.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
Each user story was tested against its acceptance criteria after implementation.

Testing included:

Testing Area Purpose Authentication Verify account creation, sign-in, password reset and account deletion Project Management Verify project creation, ownership and archiving Entry Formats Verify that project-specific fields can be created, modified and stored Rich Field Types Verify that supported field types behave correctly Entry Versions Verify that changes to formats preserve relevant historical information Computed Fields Verify calculated field behaviour Custom-Field Analysis Verify statistics and analysis using custom entry data Logbook Entries Verify that entries use the correct project entry format Time Tracking Verify that recorded time is stored and associated with the correct project Entry Browsing Verify chronological display, filtering and entry details Alternative Views Verify that entries can be represented using supported alternative views Due Dates Verify unfinished and overdue work handling Offline Capture Verify that entries can be captured without an active connection and synchronised appropriately Export/Import Verify that logbook data can be exported and imported Custom Statistics Verify that expressions evaluate correctly, reject invalid input, and saved statistics follow the data Dashboard Verify that chosen panels and their order persist per user across devices Automation Verify that rules apply only when their conditions hold, never loop, and never lose an entry Recurrence & Reminders Verify that occurrences and reminders are generated once, on time, and pushed to devices Record History Verify that every change is versioned, past states can be viewed, and restores are themselves recorded Performance Verify that entry listings page correctly and common queries stay fast Integration Verify that frontend, backend and database components work together Validation Verify that invalid or incomplete input is handled correctly Regression Testing Ensure new functionality does not break existing functionality

Testing was performed throughout development rather than being limited to the final phase. This allowed defects in individual components and interactions between features to be identified and corrected during implementation.

docs.title: Definition of Done
docs.text:
A user story is considered complete when:

  • Its acceptance criteria have been implemented.
  • The required frontend functionality is available.
  • The required backend functionality is implemented where applicable.
  • Data is correctly persisted in the database where applicable.
  • Input validation and relevant error handling are implemented.
  • The functionality has been tested successfully.
  • The implementation integrates correctly with existing functionality.
  • New functionality does not introduce known critical regressions.
  • The functionality is represented appropriately in the project documentation.

For the Intermediate phase, the Definition of Done also required the new functionality to work with the existing Basic Digital Logbook rather than functioning as isolated features. For the Advanced phase, it also required every resource to be checked against its owner, and every change to an entry to be recorded in its history.

docs.title: Development Summary
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook was developed incrementally from foundational functionality to more advanced features.

The Basic development established:

  1. Authentication and account management.
  2. Project management.
  3. Custom project entry formats.
  4. Logbook entry creation.
  5. Time tracking.
  6. Entry browsing and filtering.
  7. Integration and testing.

The Intermediate development then extended the system with:

  1. Rich field types.
  2. Entry-format modification.
  3. Entry-format version preservation.
  4. Computed fields.
  5. Custom-field analysis.
  6. Alternative entry views.
  7. Unfinished-work and due-date functionality.
  8. Offline entry capture and synchronisation.
  9. Data export and import.
  10. Integration and regression testing.

The Advanced development (Sprint 3) then added:

  1. Custom expressions and saved statistics.
  2. Entry automation rules.
  3. A personal dashboard that persists across devices.
  4. Recurring entries.
  5. Automatic reminders with push notifications.
  6. Entry version history, viewing an entry as of a date, and restoring a version.
  7. Query-performance work for large logbooks.
  8. Archiving old entries.
  9. Structured search: custom-field filters, combined filters and relevance ranking.

All Sprint 3 stories are complete.

This dependency-driven approach allowed each phase to build on previously completed functionality while reducing the risk of breaking existing project and entry data.

The development plan therefore reflects the progression from the foundational Digital Logbook requirements through the Intermediate functionality to the Advanced features, while maintaining the original system architecture and project structure.

docs.title: Purpose and scope
docs.text:
This roadmap is the delivery plan for the Digital Logbook. It connects the product brief to the user stories, team work areas, dependencies, testing and release activities. A milestone is only complete when its acceptance tests pass in the integrated application.

The agreed scope contains the Basic user stories (US00.1–US06), the Intermediate user stories (US07–US15), and the Advanced user stories (US22–US37). The brief's Advanced section gave requirements but no user stories, so the team wrote the Advanced stories and acceptance tests themselves at the start of Sprint 3 and tracked them as Gitea issues #94–#109 under the Sprint 3 - Advanced Logbook milestone.

docs.title: Roadmap completion criteria
docs.text:
The roadmap is complete when:

  • Every agreed user story, US00.1–US15 and US22–US37, has passed its acceptance tests.
  • Frontend, backend, database and migrations work together in the target environment.
  • The user can safely create, find, retain, export and restore their record of work, including any past version of an entry.
