docs.title: Initial System Design
docs.text: This page records the design as it was planned at the start of the project (August 2026). It is kept unchanged as a record of the starting point. The system has grown considerably since; §4 summarises how, and System Architecture and Database Design describe it as built.

docs.title: 1. High-Level System Architecture
docs.text: The Digital Logbook is designed as a non-monolithic web application. The system separates the user interface from the backend API and database.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The system consists of the following main components:

  • Frontend: React, Vite, and TypeScript provide the user interface.
  • Backend: Express and TypeScript provide the hand-written REST API and application logic.
  • Database: PostgreSQL, hosted using Neon, stores persistent data.
  • Prisma: Provides database access from the backend.
  • Authentication: JWT-based authentication protects authenticated API requests.
  • Email Service: Nodemailer supports email verification and password-reset functionality.
  • Shared Package: @logbook/shared contains types and validation schemas shared between the frontend and backend.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
The frontend communicates with the backend using HTTP REST requests. Authenticated requests include a JWT token.

The backend validates incoming requests using Zod before processing business logic and accessing the database through Prisma.

docs.title: 2. Component Architecture
docs.text: The application is divided into separate frontend and backend components. This separation allows the frontend and backend to be developed, tested, and deployed independently.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
The frontend is responsible for the user interface, client-side routing, form interaction, and communication with the backend API.

The main frontend components are:

  • Pages — Application screens such as Dashboard, Projects, Entries, Profile, and Settings.
  • Reusable Components — Shared interface elements such as the Sidebar, forms, modals, and page headers.
  • API Client — Uses Axios to communicate with the backend REST API.
  • Routing — React Router manages public and authenticated routes.

docs.title: Backend
docs.text:
The backend provides the application's hand-written REST API and contains the business logic.

The main backend components are:

  • Routes — Define the HTTP API endpoints.
  • Middleware — Handles authentication and request processing.
  • Validation — Zod schemas validate incoming request data.
  • Controllers — Implement application business logic.
  • Utils — Provide supporting functionality such as password hashing and email delivery.
  • Prisma — Provides access to the PostgreSQL database.

docs.title: Shared Package
docs.text: The @logbook/shared package contains common TypeScript types and Zod schemas used by both the frontend and backend. This reduces duplication and keeps the data structures used across the application consistent.

docs.title: 3. Database Design
docs.text: The Digital Logbook uses PostgreSQL as its persistent data store. Prisma ORM provides access to the database from the Express backend.

docs.title: Main Entities
docs.text: Entity Purpose User Stores student account information Project Stores projects belonging to a student EntryField Defines the custom fields available for a project LogbookEntry Stores individual logbook entries EntryValue Stores the value of a custom field for an entry PasswordReset Stores password-reset information

docs.title: Key Relationships
docs.text:
• A user can own multiple projects.
  • A project can contain multiple entry fields and logbook entries.
  • An entry contains values corresponding to the fields defined by its project.
  • Password-reset records are associated with the user who requested the reset.

docs.title: Data Integrity
docs.text: Foreign keys are used to maintain relationships between entities. Unique constraints prevent duplicate values where required, and cascading deletes support account deletion and associated data removal.

docs.title: 4. How the Design Has Evolved
docs.text:
The initial design held up: the system is still a React frontend, an Express REST API and a PostgreSQL database, with a shared types package, and the EAV entry model above still carries every project's custom fields. What changed is what was built on top of it.

Area Initial design Now Database 6 tables 23 tables: format versions, entry versions, tags, custom statistics, dashboard layouts, saved filters, automation and recurrence rules, reminders, push subscriptions, recovery codes, the Google Calendar connection, and academic modules and assessments for My Grades were added Field types Text, Number, Date, Boolean Also Tags, Checklist, Link, Reference and Computed Entry history An entry is overwritten when edited Every change is kept as a version and can be viewed or restored Authentication JWT sign-in, email verification, password reset Also TOTP two-factor authentication with recovery codes, encrypted secrets, hashed tokens and rate limiting Email Nodemailer (Gmail SMTP) Resend, with Gmail SMTP as a fallback Background work None Jobs in the API process create recurring entries, push due reminders and purge deleted accounts Frontend Pages, components, API client, routing Also a service worker for offline use and push notifications, and an offline entry queue Integrations None Google Calendar sync, web push and the Gemini-backed help assistant Deployment Not yet decided Frontend on Cloudflare Pages, backend on Render, database on Neon, CI on Gitea Actions

The request pipeline also gained an explicit ownership check: a valid token proves who the caller is, and every query is then scoped to that user's own data. See Architecture Design for the pipeline and sign-in flow.

docs.title: Design Goals
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook interface is designed to be:

  • Simple and easy for students to navigate.
  • Responsive across desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.
  • Accessible and readable.
  • Consistent across all pages.
  • Focused on quickly recording and reviewing logbook entries.
  • Flexible enough to support custom entry formats and different field types.
  • Clear when displaying deadlines, overdue work, and unfinished entries.

docs.title: Visual Direction: Calm Clarity
docs.text:
The interface was redesigned in October 2026 around one principle: a study desk, not a dashboard. Each page answers one question, and shows only what that question needs:

Page Its question Dashboard What matters to me today? Projects What am I working on, and what has gone quiet? Entries What did I do? Open Work What unfinished work needs dealing with? Board How are this project's entries organised? Calendar What's coming, and what did I log, for one project? Statistics How am I spending my time? My Grades Where do I stand in each module, and what does the rest need? Reminders What needs my attention, and why am I being reminded? Profile Who am I, and what have I been working on?

The visual language is shared across every page:

  • White cards with thin borders on a soft neutral background, and restrained shadows.
  • One accent colour, chosen by the student in Settings (blue, emerald, violet, amber or rose); every primary button, active state and highlight follows it.
  • Strong but small typography, with tabular figures so numbers line up.
  • Muted status colours. Red means only an error, a destructive action, or work that is genuinely overdue; status is always given in words and an icon as well as colour.
  • Short transitions (150–200 ms) that the operating system's reduced-motion setting turns off.
  • Light, dark and system themes, and a comfortable or compact density.

docs.title: Design Artifacts
docs.text:
The interface was designed using low-fidelity wireframes followed by a higher-fidelity mockup:

  • 📄 Wireframe — initial layout and navigation structure for each screen.
  • 📄 Mockup — refined visual design based on the wireframe.

The implemented interface follows the overall structure established by these design artifacts while incorporating additional functionality introduced during the Intermediate and Advanced phases.

docs.title: Application Navigation
docs.text:
Authenticated users reach every main area from the sidebar:

Sidebar (an inset dark panel, grouped)
├── Today
│   ├── Dashboard      what matters today, and the student's own panels
│   ├── Reminders      needs attention / upcoming / done, and reminder rules
│   └── Calendar       one project by month, Google Calendar sync
├── Work
│   ├── Projects ──► Project Detail
│   │                 ├── Entry Form
│   │                 ├── Entry Format
│   │                 ├── Entry History
│   │                 └── Automation Rules
│   ├── Entries        day by day, search, filters, saved filters, archive
│   ├── Open Work      overdue, coming up, no date yet
│   ├── Board          one project's entries in columns
│   └── Statistics     time, breakdown, over time, saved statistics
├── Academics
│   └── My Grades ──► Module page
└── Personal
    ├── Profile
    └── Settings       account, appearance, logbook, notifications, security, data

The current page is marked with an accent wash, accent text, a heavier icon and an accent edge, so it never relies on colour alone. A count of due reminders sits on Reminders, and Log out is beside the student's name. On phones the sidebar becomes a slide-in drawer, and pressing N anywhere opens a quick entry form. Offline capture works through the normal entry form.

docs.title: 1. Landing Page
docs.text:
The landing page introduces the Digital Logbook and provides options to:

  • Sign in.
  • Create an account.

See the mockup for the landing page layout.

docs.title: 2. Sign In
docs.text:
The Sign In page allows an existing student to authenticate using their account credentials.

Authentication is integrated with the rest of the application so that authenticated functionality is protected from unauthorised access.

See the mockup for the sign-in screen.

docs.title: 3. Registration
docs.text:
The Registration page allows a new student to create an account.

The interface provides the required account fields and validation before an account is created.

See the mockup for the registration screen.

docs.title: 4. Dashboard
docs.text:
The Dashboard answers "what matters today?". From the top: a greeting with New project; a short daily note; Next up (what is happening soon, grouped by day) beside On your radar (a few things worth attention, with the next step for each); Modules at a glance from My Grades; then the student's own panels.

A new account sees a getting-started guide instead of a page of empty cards: "Start with one thing you did today", with Create your first project and Import a backup, then Log your first entry once a project exists.

The student's own panels include:

  • Entry streak.
  • Deadline reminders (upcoming and overdue work).
  • Recent activity.
  • Current projects.
  • Progress over time.
  • Entries per month.
  • This week compared with last week.
  • Tags and tag ranking.
  • Recent entries.
  • The student's own saved statistics.

Students pick panels from a panel picker and arrange them with "Arrange panels". The layout is saved to their account, so the dashboard looks the same on every device. The dashboard deliberately does not repeat the figures on the Statistics page.

docs.title: 5. Projects
docs.text:
The Projects page answers "what am I working on, and what has gone quiet?". A toolbar holds search, Active / Archived / All and a grid or list layout. Each project shows its status in words (Active, Quiet after two weeks without an entry, or Archived), its entry count, time logged and last activity ("today", "24 days ago"). Edit, archive and delete sit behind one accessible More actions menu rather than a row of buttons.

Students can:

  • Create a project.
  • Open a project.
  • Edit project information.
  • Archive or unarchive a project.
  • Delete a project, after a confirmation that offers archiving instead.

Projects remain accessible after being archived, allowing students to continue managing their project data when required.

docs.title: 6. Project Detail
docs.text:
The Project Detail page provides information about a selected project.

It includes:

  • Project name and description.
  • Project entry format.
  • Project entries.
  • Recorded project time.
  • Project statistics.
  • Due-date and overdue information where applicable.
  • Options to add and manage entries.

The page acts as the main workspace for viewing the activity associated with a project.

docs.title: 7. Entry Creation and Editing
docs.text:
The entry form dynamically displays the fields defined by the selected project's entry format.

Depending on the configured entry format, students can enter different types of information, including richer field types introduced during the Intermediate phase.

The form supports:

  • Custom field values.
  • Date and time information.
  • Time spent on the entry.
  • Due dates.
  • Completion-related information.
  • Editing existing entries.
  • Live time tracking where applicable.

The form is designed to allow students to capture logbook information quickly without requiring a fixed format for every project.

Capture works from the keyboard alone:

  • N, pressed anywhere in the app while not typing in a field, opens a new entry on the project the student last worked in (or their first active project).
  • The form starts from the predictable parts of the project's last entry — its time spent, tags and repeated field values — with a note saying so. The description, links, dates and computed values start empty, and checklist items come back unticked.
  • The cursor starts in the first field of the form.
  • Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac) saves the entry.

See the wireframe and mockup for the original entry form layout.

docs.title: 8. Entry Format Management
docs.text:
The Entry Format interface allows students to define and manage the structure of their project entries.

Students can:

  • Add custom fields.
  • Define field types.
  • Modify existing entry formats.
  • Work with richer field types.
  • Use computed fields where configured.
  • Preserve previous entry-format versions when formats are modified.

This allows different projects to use entry structures that match their specific requirements.

docs.title: 9. Entries
docs.text:
The Entries page answers "what did I do?", as a logbook grouped by day with each day's total time. Four compact figures sit at the top (this week, time this week, streak, all time). One filter bar holds search, project and sort order; less common filters (this week or overdue, archive, a project's own fields, tags) open under Filters, and combinations can be saved.

Students can:

  • Browse entries day by day, newest or oldest first.
  • Search across their entries and fields, and narrow to one project.
  • Combine filters, save them, and clear them.
  • Open an entry to view or edit it.
  • See an entry's due date as quiet context, without entries being treated as tasks.

The interface is designed to make previously recorded work easy to locate and review.

docs.title: 10. Alternative Entry Views
docs.text:
Besides the Entries timeline, two views organise one project's entries:

  • Board — entries in columns, grouped by status (open or done) or by any of the project's own fields; entries without a value sit in a quieter Not grouped column. Each column shows its count.
  • Calendar — a month of due dates and logged entries (a list on phones), starting the week on the day chosen in Settings, with Google Calendar sync.

docs.title: 11. Due Dates and Overdue Work
docs.text:
Entries can include due dates to help students track unfinished work.

The interface provides visual information for entries that are approaching or have passed their deadlines.

Students can identify:

  • Entries with upcoming deadlines.
  • Overdue entries.
  • Unfinished work.
  • Completed work.

Open Work is the page that owns unfinished work: Overdue (with how late each item is), Coming up (the next two weeks, grouped by day, then later) and No date yet. Each item can be marked done or given a new date in place.

docs.title: 12. Profile and Settings
docs.text:
The Profile and Settings area allows students to manage their account and application preferences.

It provides access to account-related functionality and application settings, including:

  • Profile information.
  • Account management.
  • Theme preferences.
  • Data export.
  • Data import.
  • Other application settings.

The application supports light, dark, and system theme preferences.

Settings also turns reminder notifications on for the current device, and holds the two-factor authentication setup, including recovery codes.

See the mockup for the profile and settings layout.

docs.title: 13. Offline Capture
docs.text:
The interface supports capturing logbook entries when the student temporarily does not have a reliable connection.

Offline entries can be stored locally and synchronised when connectivity becomes available again.

The interface is designed to make offline capture consistent with the normal entry-creation workflow so that students do not need to use a separate interface.

docs.title: 14. Data Export and Import
docs.text:
The Settings area provides functionality for exporting and importing logbook data.

This allows students to:

  • Export their logbook information for backup or portability.
  • Import previously exported logbook data.
  • Retain their project and entry information when moving or restoring data.

The import/export functionality is integrated into the existing application rather than requiring users to interact directly with the database.

docs.title: 15. Statistics
docs.text:
The Statistics page answers "how am I spending my time?": time logged across all projects, then — for a chosen project — a Breakdown (measure, calculate, group by) and Over time (per day, week or month, with real period labels).

Students can also write their own expression, such as SUM({Hours}) / COUNT(), see its result immediately, and save it as a named statistic that sits beside the built-in ones and can be added to the dashboard. An expression that cannot be worked out explains why rather than showing a wrong number.

docs.title: 16. Reminders
docs.text:
The Reminders page has three tabs — Needs attention, Upcoming and Done & dismissed — and every reminder says why it exists: set by the student, or which rule made it. Complete is the main action, then Snooze 1 day and Dismiss; students can create their own.

The reminder rules on the same page switch on automatic reminders for upcoming due dates, overdue entries, entries left untouched, and a daily prompt when nothing has been logged. With notifications turned on, reminders appear as system notifications, even when the logbook is closed.

docs.title: 17. Entry History
docs.text: From an entry, students open its history: every saved version, oldest first, with what changed shown field by field against the current version. They can view the entry as it was on a chosen date, and restore an earlier version after confirming. A restore is added to the history rather than replacing it.

docs.title: 18. Automation Rules
docs.text: On a project's page, students create rules of the form "when an entry is created or saved and these conditions hold, add or remove a tag or set the status". Only the conditions that make sense for each field type are offered. Rules can be edited, switched off and deleted.

docs.title: 19. Recurring Entries and Archiving
docs.text: When creating an entry, students can make it repeat daily, weekly or monthly, and later stop it repeating. On the Entries page, old entries can be moved to the archive individually or in bulk, viewed there, and brought back.

docs.title: 20. My Grades
docs.text:
My Grades answers "where do I stand in each module, and what does the rest of it need?". Next assessment sits at the top. Each module card shows, from the grade engine:

  • how many assessments are marked and remaining, and how much of the module's weight that is;
  • the average on marked work and the points secured toward the final mark out of 100, kept as two separate figures;
  • a bar of secured, still possible and no-longer-possible weight, with the target marked;
  • one sentence for the target, such as "You need 80.0% on the remaining 50% to reach 70%".

Every figure is weighted by each assessment's own weight. A module whose weights don't add up says so instead of showing figures worked out on the wrong weights.

docs.title: 21. Profile
docs.text: The Profile is an identity card — photo or initial, name, degree and year, email, student number — with entries, time logged and streak; then twelve weeks of activity as a heatmap whose every day is labelled for screen readers; then recent projects and the tags used most.

docs.title: 22. Help Assistant
docs.text: A help button on every page opens a short chat that answers "how do I…?" questions about the logbook and offers a button to the right page. It is backed by Google's Gemini API; see the AI Help Assistant for how it works.

docs.title: Responsive Design
docs.text: The interface follows a responsive design approach so that the application remains usable across different screen sizes.

docs.title: Desktop
docs.text:
A sidebar navigation is used alongside the main content area.

The larger screen provides enough space for dashboards, project information, entry lists, and forms to be displayed simultaneously where appropriate.

docs.title: Tablet
docs.text:
The navigation and content areas adapt to the smaller screen width.

Layouts adjust to prevent unnecessary horizontal scrolling while maintaining access to the main application functionality.

docs.title: Mobile
docs.text:
The sidebar can be collapsed or replaced with a mobile navigation menu.

Forms, entry fields, project information, and lists use the available screen width so that core functionality remains accessible on smaller devices.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
The interface follows modern accessibility practices, including:

  • Semantic HTML elements.
  • Keyboard-accessible controls.
  • Labels for form inputs.
  • Sufficient colour contrast.
  • Visible focus states.
  • Descriptive button and link text.
  • Responsive layouts.
  • Clear visual distinction between different entry states.
  • Accessible form validation and feedback where applicable.

Animations respect the operating system's reduced-motion setting.

Concretely, across the redesigned pages:

  • Every page has one h1 and sections named by their headings, so screen readers can jump between them; a Skip to content link comes first.
  • The current sidebar page carries aria-current="page"; tabs use role="tab" with arrow-key movement; switches use role="switch" with aria-checked; menus open, move and close from the keyboard.
  • Icon-only buttons have accessible names; charts and grade bars have text alternatives (role="img" labels, a progressbar with its value in words); every heatmap day is labelled.
  • Status is never colour alone: overdue, quiet, archived, completed and dismissed each have words and an icon.
  • A visible focus ring follows the accent colour on the page and a light ring on the dark sidebar.
  • Small helper text is darkened on light backgrounds to meet a 4.5:1 contrast ratio.

docs.title: Design Consistency
docs.text:
The application uses consistent layouts, navigation patterns, controls, and visual conventions across its main screens.

Common functionality such as creating, editing, viewing, and filtering entries follows the same interaction patterns throughout the application.

This consistency reduces the amount of navigation and relearning required when students move between projects, entries, and account settings.

Each document explains what the feature does, why we added it, and how it is implemented, from the user interface through the API to the database and any external service.

docs.text:
• Source files are referred to by their path from the repository root, such as apps/backend/src/utils/assistant.ts, as in the rest of docs/.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
A floating "Ask for help" chat button appears on every signed-in page. A student types a question about using the app ("How do I make an entry repeat?") and gets a short answer generated by Google's Gemini API. When one page of the app answers the question, the reply comes with a "Take me to …" button that navigates there.

The assistant only answers questions about Digital Logbook, and it never sees the student's logbook data.

docs.title: 2. Problem / Motivation
docs.text:
The app has grown to many pages: projects, entries, open work, stats, calendar, board, reminders, My Grades, profile and settings, each with several tools. In Round 1 user testing, one of six testers struggled to find the Calendar and Board views (tracked as FEAT-003, view discoverability). A student who cannot find a feature effectively does not have it.

The commit that introduced the assistant describes its purpose as helping students "find their way around the app": instead of searching the sidebar, they can ask in their own words and be taken to the right page. (FEAT-003 itself, which proposes navigation hints and a guided tour, remains a separate open issue.)

docs.title: 3. What It Does
docs.text:
• A round button in the corner of every signed-in page opens a chat panel.
  • The panel offers four suggested questions to start with, for example "Where do I set up reminders?".
  • The student's question, together with the earlier turns of the conversation, is answered in two to five sentences or a few steps, naming the exact page and button to use.
  • If the answer is a page, a "Take me to Reminders" (or similar) button appears under the reply. It is hidden when the student is already on that page.
  • Off-topic questions are politely declined.
  • If the assistant is not configured, busy or rate-limited, the panel shows the server's explanation and puts the question back in the text box, so it can be sent again without being sent twice.
  • Enter sends; Shift+Enter adds a new line; Escape closes the panel.
  • The conversation lasts until the page is reloaded; it is not stored.

docs.title: 4. How It Works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Student (browser)
    participant F as HelpAssistant.tsx
    participant B as Backend /api/assistant/chat
    participant G as Gemini API
    S->>F: types a question
    F->>B: POST { messages, currentPath } + JWT
    B->>B: requireAuth, rate limit, validate (Zod)
    B->>G: system instruction (app guide + current page) + conversation,<br/>JSON response schema
    alt model busy / out of quota
        G-->>B: 429 / 503
        B->>G: same request to the next model
    end
    G-->>B: { "reply": "...", "navigateTo": "/reminders" }
    B->>B: parse JSON, check navigateTo against the allowlist
    B-->>F: { reply, navigateTo }
    F-->>S: answer + "Take me to …" button
  1. Browser. HelpAssistant.tsx sends the whole conversation so far plus the current route (location.pathname) to POST /api/assistant/chat through the shared Axios client, which attaches the student's JWT.
  2. Backend checks. The route requires a signed-in student (requireAuth), applies a dedicated rate limit, and validates the body with Zod before anything is sent to Google.
  3. Prompt. The backend builds a Gemini request: a fixed system instruction describing the app, plus the student's current page, plus the conversation.
  4. Structured output. Gemini is asked to reply in a fixed JSON shape: an answer, and at most one page from a fixed list.
  5. Validation and fallback. The backend parses the JSON, discards any page that is not a real route, and, if a model is busy, retries with the next configured model.
  6. Display. The frontend shows the reply and, when there is a page, a button that calls React Router's navigate().

docs.title: 5. Technical Implementation
docs.text:
Layer File Responsibility UI apps/frontend/src/components/HelpAssistant.tsx Floating button, chat panel, suggested questions, "Take me to" button, error display UI mount apps/frontend/src/components/AppLayout.tsx Renders the assistant once inside the signed-in layout, so it is on every app page API client apps/frontend/src/api.ts (askAssistant) POST /assistant/chat Route apps/backend/src/routes/assistant.routes.ts POST /api/assistant/chat behind requireAuth and assistantLimiter Controller apps/backend/src/controllers/assistant.controller.ts 503 when unconfigured, 400 on invalid input, 502 when no model answers Validation apps/backend/src/schemas/assistant.schema.ts Conversation shape and size limits AI logic apps/backend/src/utils/assistant.ts App guide, request building, Gemini calls, model fallback, response parsing Rate limit apps/backend/src/middleware/rateLimit.middleware.ts (assistantLimiter) Questions per window per IP address Tests apps/backend/src/__tests__/assistant.test.ts, apps/frontend/src/components/__tests__/HelpAssistant.test.tsx Gemini is mocked; no real API calls in tests

No database tables are involved, and no new npm dependency: the backend calls Gemini's REST endpoint with Node's built-in fetch.

docs.title: AI-specific details
docs.text:
Provider and endpoint. Google's Gemini API, called over REST at https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/<model>:generateContent. The API key is sent in the x-goog-api-key header from the backend only; the browser never sees it.

Model(s). By default the backend tries gemini-flash-lite-latest, then gemini-3.1-flash-lite. The list can be replaced with the GEMINI_MODEL environment variable (comma-separated, tried in order).

Why this provider and these models. The code and configuration record that the free tier is enough for this use (apps/backend/.env.example), and that the "lite" models are the ones a free-tier key can use reliably (apps/backend/src/utils/assistant.ts). Gemini also supports a JSON response schema, which the "Take me to" button depends on (see below). A comparison with other providers is not recorded in the repository.

What is sent to the AI. Only:

  • the conversation in the chat panel (the student's questions and the assistant's earlier answers), at most the last 20 messages, each at most 1,000 characters;
  • the route the student is currently on, e.g. /reminders;
  • the fixed app guide (below).

No logbook data (projects, entries, grades), no name, email or account id is sent. The code records why: the free Gemini tier may use prompts to improve Google's models.

How the prompt is constructed. buildRequest() in assistant.ts sends:

  • systemInstruction: the constant APP_GUIDE text plus "The student is currently on <path>." APP_GUIDE tells the model its role, to be brief, to name exact pages and buttons, to answer only about this app, and never to invent features. It then describes every page and its controls. Because it is written by hand, it must be updated whenever a feature is added (it was, for example, extended for My Grades).
  • contents: the conversation, each message tagged user or model.
  • generationConfig: temperature: 0.3 (consistent, factual answers), maxOutputTokens: 600, responseMimeType: "application/json" and a responseSchema requiring reply (a string) and navigateTo (one of "none" or the allowed app routes).

How the response is processed. parseModelOutput():

  • parses the JSON; if the model ignored the format, the raw text is still used as the answer;
  • keeps navigateTo only if it is in NAVIGABLE_PATHS, the list of real routes, so the model can never send a student to a page that does not exist;
  • treats an empty answer as a failure, so the next model is tried.

Error and fallback behaviour.

Situation Behaviour GEMINI_API_KEY not set 503 "The help assistant is not set up on this server." Invalid conversation (empty, too long, not ending with a question) 400 with the reason Too many questions from one address 429 from the rate limiter (default 30 per 10 minutes, configurable) A model answers 404, 429, 500 or 503, or returns nothing The next model is tried Any other error, or every model failed 502 "The assistant couldn't answer right now…" A model takes more than 20 seconds The request is aborted and treated as a failure

In every error case the frontend shows the message and keeps the typed question.

Security and privacy.

  • The API key lives only in the backend environment (GEMINI_API_KEY); the frontend talks to our backend, never to Google directly.
  • Only signed-in students can use the endpoint, and it is rate-limited to protect the shared free-tier quota.
  • No personal or logbook data is sent (see above).
  • The model's output cannot cause navigation outside the allowlisted routes.
  • Input size is capped (20 messages × 1,000 characters).

Example interaction. The exchange below shows the format; the exact wording of a live answer comes from the model and varies.

Student: Where do I set up reminders?

Assistant: Open Reminders and press New reminder. Your reminder rules, such as how many days before a due date to remind you, are on the same page.

[Take me to Reminders]

The backend receives {"reply": "...", "navigateTo": "/reminders"} from Gemini and returns the same shape to the browser.

docs.title: 6. User Workflow / Demonstration
docs.text:
1. Sign in; any app page shows the round help button in the corner.
  2. Click it. The panel opens with suggested questions.
  3. Click "Where do I set up reminders?" or type a question.
  4. Read the answer; click Take me to Reminders. On a computer the panel stays open on the new page; on a phone-sized screen it closes so the page is visible. The conversation is kept either way.
  5. Ask a follow-up ("And how do I turn on notifications?"); the earlier turns are sent too, so the assistant understands "and".
  6. Ask something unrelated ("What's the capital of France?") to see it decline.

docs.text:
Add these files under docs/extra-features/images/ai-help-assistant/, then remove the comment markers around each image.

docs.title: 8. Limitations
docs.text:
• Accuracy depends on the hand-written app guide. A feature missing from APP_GUIDE is unknown to the assistant, and the model may still phrase an answer imperfectly.
  • Two lists to keep in step. The pages the assistant may point to (NAVIGABLE_PATHS in the backend) and the names on its buttons (PAGE_NAMES in HelpAssistant.tsx) are separate lists. A page added to the first but not the second shows its path, such as "/grades", instead of its name.
  • Free-tier limits. Shared quota can run out; the fallback model helps but cannot guarantee an answer. Free-tier prompts may be used by Google to improve its models, which is why no logbook data is sent.
  • The rate limit is per IP address, so students behind one network address share it.
  • No memory between visits. The conversation is lost on reload.
  • Answers are not streamed; the student waits for the whole reply.
  • Help only. It cannot perform actions or read the student's own data, so it cannot answer "what is due tomorrow?".

docs.title: 9. Future Improvements
docs.text:
• Share one list of pages between the backend allowlist and the frontend's button names, so they cannot drift apart.
  • Generate parts of APP_GUIDE from the route list, so new pages cannot be forgotten.
  • Stream answers for a faster feel.
  • With explicit consent and a paid tier that does not train on prompts, allow questions about the student's own data.
  • Add the guided tour proposed in FEAT-003 alongside the assistant.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text: A student can connect their own Google account from the Calendar page and copy the due dates of their open logbook entries into their primary Google Calendar as all-day events. Syncing again brings the calendar up to date: changed dates are moved, and finished, archived or deleted entries are removed.

docs.title: 2. Problem / Motivation
docs.text: Due dates in the logbook are only useful if the student sees them. Most students already live in Google Calendar for lectures and tests, so a deadline that exists only inside the app is easy to miss. The feature was tracked as FEAT-001 with the story: "As a student, I want my logbook entry deadlines to appear on my Google Calendar so that I get timely reminders alongside my other commitments."

docs.title: 3. What It Does
docs.text:
On the Calendar page, a Google Calendar panel offers:

  • Connect Google Calendar: sends the student to Google to grant access, then back to the Calendar page with a "connected" message.
  • Sync now: creates, updates or removes calendar events, then reports the result, e.g. "Synced: 2 added, 1 updated, 1 removed."
  • Disconnect: removes the connection. Events already added stay in the student's calendar.

Each event is an all-day event on the due date, titled <Project name> — <entry's first text value>, with a link back to the project in its description. Only open, unarchived entries that have a due date are synced — the same work the Open Work page lists.

A sync with nothing to change reports "Everything is already up to date." If the server has not been configured for Google, the API answers 503, the Connect button is disabled and the panel explains that sync is not set up on the server yet. If the status check itself fails (for example offline), the panel says so and offers Try again instead.

docs.title: 4. How It Works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Student
    participant F as GoogleCalendarSync.tsx
    participant B as Backend /api/google-calendar
    participant G as Google (OAuth + Calendar API)
    S->>F: Connect
    F->>B: GET /connect (JWT)
    B-->>F: Google consent URL with signed state
    F->>G: browser goes to Google's consent screen
    G->>B: GET /callback?code&state
    B->>B: verify state → user; exchange code for tokens;<br/>encrypt and store tokens
    B-->>S: redirect to /calendar?calendar=connected
    S->>F: Sync now
    F->>B: POST /sync (JWT)
    B->>G: list our events; insert / patch / delete
    B-->>F: { created, updated, removed }

Connecting (OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow).

  1. GET /api/google-calendar/connect (signed in) builds Google's consent URL with:
  2. the calendar.events scope only;
  3. access_type: "offline" and prompt: "consent", so Google issues a refresh token;
  4. a state value.
  5. The state is a short-lived (10-minute) JWT naming the student, with purpose: "oauth-state". Google's redirect back to /callback is a plain browser navigation without our login token, so the state is the only thing tying the returned code to the right account. A forged or expired state is rejected, and a state token can't be used as a login token (or the other way round).
  6. /callback exchanges the code for tokens, encrypts them and stores them in the GoogleCalendarConnection row for that student, then redirects to /calendar?calendar=connected (or denied / error).

Syncing. POST /api/google-calendar/sync:

  1. decrypts the stored tokens. If they can't be decrypted, for example because the encryption key changed, the connection is deleted and the student is asked to connect again (409);
  2. lets the Google client refresh an expired access token, and saves the new one, encrypted;
  3. runs syncDueDates.

docs.title: 5. Technical Implementation
docs.text:
Layer File Responsibility UI apps/frontend/src/components/GoogleCalendarSync.tsx (shown on CalendarPage.tsx) Status, connect, sync, disconnect, result messages Routes apps/backend/src/routes/googleCalendarRoutes.ts GET /connect, GET /callback, GET /status, POST /sync, DELETE /disconnect under /api/google-calendar Sync logic apps/backend/src/services/googleCalendarService.ts OAuth client per request, syncDueDates Token encryption apps/backend/src/utils/googleTokens.ts AES-256-GCM encrypt/decrypt OAuth state apps/backend/src/utils/auth.ts (generateOAuthState, verifyOAuthState) Signed, purpose-scoped, 10-minute state Database GoogleCalendarConnection model in apps/backend/prisma/schema.prisma One row per student: encrypted access and refresh tokens, expiry Library googleapis (see docs/third-party.md) OAuth code exchange, token refresh, Calendar API. Only the Calendar module is imported; the package root's type definitions for every Google API made the backend build run out of memory Tests apps/backend/src/__tests__/googleCalendar.test.ts, googleCalendarSync.test.ts State, encryption, callback, sync; Google is mocked

The sync algorithm (syncDueDates) is idempotent and stores no Google event ids:

  1. Every event the logbook creates carries private extended properties logbookSource=digital-logbook and logbookEntryId=<entry id>. These are visible only to this OAuth client.
  2. On sync, it lists only events with logbookSource=digital-logbook (following pagination) and indexes them by entry id.
  3. For each open, dated entry it either inserts a new event, patches an event whose title, description or date changed, or leaves an unchanged one alone.
  4. Any logbook event left over belongs to an entry that was finished, undated, archived or deleted, or is a duplicate; it is deleted. "Already gone" (404, 410) counts as success.
  5. It returns { created, updated, removed }.

Because the events identify themselves, re-running sync never duplicates events, and nothing in our database has to be kept in step with Google.

Security points.

  • Tokens are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, a fresh IV each time and an authentication tag, so tampering is detected. The key is derived from the GOOGLE_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY environment variable.
  • A new OAuth client is created per request, so one student's credentials can never leak into another's request.
  • The narrow calendar.events scope is requested, not full calendar access.
  • Disconnecting also tries to revoke the grant at Google, so the app disappears from the student's Google third-party access list. The local removal happens even if revocation fails.

Configuration (names only; values are environment secrets): GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI, GOOGLE_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and APP_URL for the redirect back to the Calendar page.

docs.title: 6. User Workflow / Demonstration
docs.text:
1. Create an entry with a due date in any project.
  2. Open Calendar and press Connect Google Calendar.
  3. Choose a Google account and allow access to calendar events; you return to the Calendar page with "Google Calendar connected".
  4. Press Sync now: "Synced: 1 added". Open Google Calendar to see an all-day event on the due date, titled with the project and entry.
  5. Change the entry's due date and press Sync now: "1 updated", and the event moves.
  6. Mark the entry done and sync again: "1 removed".
  7. Press Disconnect: the connection is removed; existing events stay.

docs.title: 8. Limitations
docs.text:
• Sync is manual. Events change only when the student presses Sync now. FEAT-001 proposed syncing automatically on every entry change; that is not how it was built.
  • One-way. Changes made in Google Calendar are not brought back into the logbook.
  • Primary calendar only, and only entry due dates. Assessment dates from My Grades are not synced.
  • Events stay after disconnecting. The student removes them in Google Calendar themselves.
  • Requires server configuration (Google Cloud OAuth client and the variables above). Without it, Connect is disabled.
  • Who can connect also depends on how the OAuth consent screen is set up in Google Cloud. For example, an app still in Google's "testing" mode only allows listed test users. That setting is outside the repository.
  • Rotating the encryption key makes stored tokens unreadable; affected students are asked to connect again.

docs.text:

  • Include My Grades assessment dates (tests and due dates).
  • Let the student choose a calendar, or create a dedicated "Digital Logbook" calendar.
  • Offer to remove the logbook's events when disconnecting.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
My Grades lets a student track their university modules and the assessments that make up each mark. For every module it shows how many marks are already secured, the student's average on marked work, how much of the module is marked and remaining, the mark needed on the rest to reach a target, whether that target is still reachable, and a what-if calculator. Assessments can carry a due or test date, which feeds an upcoming list and reminders 5 days and 2 days before.

It is reached from My Grades in the sidebar (/grades).

docs.title: 2. Problem / Motivation
docs.text:
In SUS Round 2 the one substantive "one change" suggestion was a "year to date calculator or tracking of grades" (docs/user-feedback.md; tracked as FEAT-009). Students already work out these figures by hand or in spreadsheets, and the common mistakes are exactly the ones the app can prevent:

  • mixing up a mark out of a maximum (25 / 40) with a percentage (62.5%);
  • confusing points secured (45 out of 100) with performance so far (75% on the 60% that has been marked). A student on 45 points with 60% marked is doing well, not failing;
  • full-year modules, where each semester's assessments total 100% within the semester, and the semesters are then weighted (60/40, 50/50 …) into the module. That is two separate levels of weighting.

docs.title: 3. What It Does
docs.text:
Overview page (/grades)

  • An Upcoming strip of dated, unmarked assessments in the next 14 days, with countdowns ("In 3 days · Test").
  • An Academic year dropdown built from the years the student actually has modules in, plus All years. Nothing is hard-coded: a new year appears as soon as a module exists for it.
  • All / Semester 1 / Semester 2 filters; full-year modules appear under both semesters.
  • A card per module: Secured X / 100, Average on marked work, a marked / remaining bar, and the target status, or Finish setting up while the weights do not add up.

Module page (/grades/:moduleId)

  • Four tiles: Secured, Average on marked work, Marked, Remaining. There is deliberately no ambiguous "current mark".
  • The assessments: weight, the mark exactly as entered with its conversion (25 / 40 = 62.5%), its contribution in points (25.0 pts), a status badge (Marked, Missed, Not marked yet, Awaiting mark), and its date. Full-year modules are grouped by semester, with each semester's weight, mark and points.
  • Weight checks: "Weights total 90% — 10% unassigned". An incomplete setup can be saved, but What do I need? and What if? stay off until it is fixed, so they never calculate on wrong weights.
  • What do I need?: choose a target (Pass 50%, 60%, 70%, 75% or custom) to see the average needed on the remaining work, rounded up, with the assumption stated, plus the highest possible final mark and a status: Secured, Within reach, Stretch, Not reachable, Not enough data or No target.
  • What if?: a slider ("If I average 60% on everything left") or a mark per remaining assessment, giving a projected final mark. It is labelled Hypothetical — not saved, and with one assessment left it shows a table (40% → 61%, 50% → 65% …).
  • How is this calculated?: the working, line by line, with the student's own numbers.
  • Add, edit and delete modules and assessments. Deleting a module asks for confirmation and removes its assessments too.

Reminders. A dated assessment produces a reminder 5 days before and another 2 days before, on the existing Reminders page and as notifications when those are switched on. They can be turned off per assessment, or for all assessments with the "Upcoming tests & assessments" rule.

docs.title: 4. How It Works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    UI["GradesPage / GradeModulePage<br/>(React)"] -- "api.ts" --> API["/api/grades<br/>(Express)"]
    API -- Prisma --> DB[("academic_modules<br/>assessments")]
    UI -- "module + assessments as entered" --> ENG["computeModule()<br/>lib/grades.ts"]
    ENG -- "secured, average, required,<br/>status, projection, working" --> UI
    GEN["generateReminders()<br/>(existing reminder rules)"] -- reads --> DB
    GEN --> REM[("reminders")]
    REM --> RP["Reminders page,<br/>push / in-app notifications"]
  1. The API stores and returns only what the student entered: weights, the mark as 25 / 40 or 62.5%, missed, dates. It calculates nothing.
  2. In the browser, every figure comes from one pure function, computeModule(module, { target, hypothetical }). The cards, tiles, target panel, what-if projection and explanation all read its result, so they can never disagree, and the UI contains no grade arithmetic of its own.
  3. What-if calls the same function with hypothetical marks filled in for unmarked assessments. Real marks are never overridden and nothing is saved.
  4. Reminders are produced by the app's existing reminder generator, which gained one rule; there is no second notification system.

docs.title: The calculation engine: apps/frontend/src/lib/grades.ts
docs.text:
Pure TypeScript: no React, no network, no dates. Problems are reported as setup.issues, never thrown.

  • Two weighting levels. An assessment's weight is its share of its section. A semester module has one section worth 100; a full-year module has Semester 1 and Semester 2, where only Semester 1's weight is stored and Semester 2 is 100 − S1, so they always total 100 and there is no 50/50 default. Each assessment's effective weight is the product of the two (40% of a Semester 1 worth 60% is 24% of the module).
  • Core formulas, all on effective weights: contribution = percent × effectiveWeight / 100; secured = Σ contributions (missed counts as 0); average = secured / markedWeight × 100; required = (target − secured) / remainingWeight × 100; highest possible = secured + remainingWeight.
  • Target status, first match wins: Secured (secured ≥ target) → Not reachable (required > 100, or nothing left) → Not enough data (nothing marked) → Within reach (required ≤ average) → Stretch. A required mark is only reported when it is achievable, so the UI never shows a negative or above-100 requirement.
  • Setup rules. A section's weights must total 100 (within 0.01, so 33.33 × 3 counts); a section with no assessments yet counts as fully remaining, so targets work during Semester 1 before Semester 2 is set up. Weights are never silently normalised.
  • Rounding happens only in the engine's display helpers: one decimal place, the required mark rounded up, and a small tolerance for floating-point noise (100 − 99.99 is 0.0100000000000051 in JavaScript).
  • Explanation data (summary.explanation): the "How is this calculated?" panel renders these lines instead of recomputing anything.

docs.title: Reminders (inside the existing pipeline)
docs.text:
• When: for each unmarked, not-missed assessment with remind on and a date within 5 days. The 5-day reminder covers 5 to 3 days before; the 2-day reminder covers 2 days before to the day itself.
  • Keys: each reminder has a stable key, assessment:<id>:<date>:<5|2>. Together with the existing unique (user, ruleKey) index this means re-running the rules never duplicates a reminder, and each is pushed once.
  • Titles name the date rather than counting down: "Test on Sun 15 Nov: COMS3011A Final Test", "Due Fri 13 Nov: …".
  • Timing: new reminders appear from 08:00 in the student's time zone, so no notification arrives overnight.
  • Cleanup uses the generator's existing rules. A marked or missed assessment completes its reminder. A moved or passed date, or a switched-off rule, removes it. Deleting the assessment deletes it.

docs.title: 6. User Workflow / Demonstration
docs.text:
1. Open My Grades from the sidebar and press Add module: code COMS3011A, name, academic year, Semester module, Semester 2.
  2. Add assessments: Midterm, weight 40, Mark out of 25 / 40 (the form shows "Recorded as 25 / 40 = 62.5%"); Tutorial 1, 10, 10 / 10; Tutorial 2, 10, 100%; Exam, 40, no mark, with a date and Test or exam date.
  3. The tiles read Secured 45.0 / 100, Average 75.0%, Marked 60.0%, Remaining 40.0%.
  4. In What do I need? choose Pass (50%): "You need 12.5% on the remaining 40% to finish with 50%", status Within reach.
  5. In What if? drag to 60%: projected final mark 69.0%, labelled hypothetical. The table lists 40% → 61.0% … 80% → 77.0%.
  6. Open How is this calculated? to see each line of the working.
  7. Add a full-year module with S1 60 / S2 40 to see the two weighting levels: a Semester 1 test at 40% shows "24% of module".
  8. Back on the overview, the exam appears in Upcoming; 5 days before it, a reminder appears on the Reminders page.

docs.title: 8. Limitations
docs.text:
• Unofficial estimate. University rules such as exam subminimums, DP requirements, "best N of M" tutorials, excused assessments, bonus marks and supplementary exams are not modelled; the pages say so.
  • The required mark assumes the same mark on every remaining assessment; the UI states this next to the figure.
  • Changes need a connection. Grades can be viewed offline from the cache but not edited offline.
  • Not in export/import yet, so restoring a backup does not include grades.
  • No GPA or year average; the correct Wits rules would need to be confirmed first.
  • Live-site deployment: the reminder type ASSESSMENT requires the backend that includes this feature. An older deployed backend should not run against a database that holds such reminders.
